articles.headline: Verstappen wins extraordinary race as Ferraris collide
keyFacts: Max Verstappen won the Las Vegas Grand Prix after a race characterized by constant lead changes and intense competition.
Mercedes driver George Russell crashed late in the race, while Ferrari drivers Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton both received 10-second penalties for collisions.
Formula 1 will continue its season next weekend at the Qatar Grand Prix held at the Lusail International Circuit.
body: The Las Vegas Grand Prix featured 'yo-yo racing' throughout the field with regular overtaking [Reuters] Red Bull's Max Verstappen won an extraordinary Las Vegas Grand Prix that saw a non-stop battle for the lead for the entire race.
The leading group of 10 cars were tied together for the vast majority of the race as the lead constantly changed hands between Verstappen and the Mercedes drivers George Russell and Kimi Antonelli.
But Verstappen was the one constant, always seeming a step ahead of his rivals as he debated electrical energy deployment strategy with his team.

And in the final laps, Mercedes' challenge unravelled as first Russell made a mistake and crashed trying to pass Antonelli and the Italian lost out to the two McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri going into the final lap.
The world champion dropped to fifth going on to the Strip on the last lap but was able to reclaim the place from Alpine's Pierre Gasly at the end of the long straight.
And there was more drama at Ferrari as Charles Leclerc earned a 10-second penalty for tipping Lewis Hamilton into a spin.
Earlier, Hamilton had been given a 10-second penalty of his own for passing Norris off the track in a fight for position that also involved Leclerc.

It was a grand prix more reminiscent of American oval racing than Formula 1, and it depended on unique circumstances revolving around the Las Vegas circuit and energy starved hybrid engines this year.
But there was no questioning the showbiz value in the city that prides itself as the entertainment capital of the world.
The key stories of an engrossing race were:
Verstappen's remarkable intelligence and control in the lead in the most demanding of circumstances
Another dip in a dreadful season for Russell
More controversy at Ferrari, as both drivers earned 10-second penalties for driving infringements in battles involving the other
Verstappen in control despite lead changes

Challengers came and went but Max Verstappen was never without the lead for long in Las Vegas [Getty Images] "How many overtakes did I do?" Verstappen asked his engineer on the slowing down lap, as he reflected on a race the like of which F1 has not seen since the famous Monza slipstreaming battles of the 1960s and early 1970s.
"Yeah, and not many of them on the straight," his new engineer Tom Hart said, summing up how Verstappen had secured the win against the Mercedes challenge.
Lap after lap after lap, Verstappen, who started from pole, would lose the lead to Russell on the Strip only to reclaim it at the last corner, usually going around the outside.
If that did not work, and Russell passed later in the lap, or led across the line, Verstappen developed a trademark move around the outside of Turn Three to get back in front.
The race went on and on like that, punctuated by a mid-grand prix safety car, but through it all Verstappen always seemed in control.
As the race wore on, Antonelli came into the picture after starting sixth, and passed Russell with 12 laps to go to become Verstappen's main challenger.
Now it was the Italian's turn to swap places with Verstappen, but again the Dutchman had the measure of Mercedes.
At one point, Verstappen asked his team to come up with a better deployment strategy for the final lap because he thought Mercedes had "figured it out".
They came back to him to say that he had already come up with the best approach.
In the end, though, he need not have worried, as his rivals behind him gave him enough of a gap at the start of the final lap to not have to worry too much about defending his lead.
Charles Leclerc (right) dropped to 10th as a result of being given a 10-second penalty for colliding with Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton [Getty Images] Verstappen laughs at Russell error
That critical final phase started with Russell deciding to make a move to become Verstappen's challenger again.

Russell went for a move into Turn Five with two laps to go but he locked up his brakes over the bumps heading into the corner - bumps that had earlier taken Red Bull's Isack Hadjar out of the lead battle when his front wing broke over them - and went straight on into the barrier.
Russell managed to reverse out of the barrier but a ninth place finish was not what he was expecting.
The incident was also unfortunate for him in the context of his calling out Verstappen's driving after qualifying, when he said "somebody has got to stand up to that guy".
Verstappen had the last word, both on track and literally. After seeing Russell's embarrassing mistake, Verstappen came on the radio to say: "Hah, hah. Well done. My God."
Now Antonelli looked to be the man who would challenge Verstappen for the win.

But that was counting without the McLarens. Piastri had already driven an outstanding race to recover from starting 17th because of an engine penalty and Norris had at one point dropped out of the top 10 in the chaotic lead battle in the first part of the grand prix.

But they were third and fourth around the penultimate lap and in what looked like a co-ordinated attack but certainly wasn't, both swept around Antonelli around the outside of the fast final corner heading into the last lap.
That gave Verstappen breathing space, and Antonelli was delayed sufficiently that he could not recover to challenge them.
Second-placed Norris summed it up, saying: "I think that must have been the most chaotic race ever in the history of Formula 1. I didn't know what was happening half the time."

articles.headline: Tomorrow's Top 25 Today: Ohio State, Indiana, UCLA fall in college football rankings amid Big Ten chaos
keyFacts: Big Ten teams Ohio State, Indiana, and UCLA all suffered losses to unranked opponents during Week 12 of the college football season.
These upsets significantly impacted the Big Ten title race and the overall College Football Playoff rankings.
AP voters are expected to release updated rankings on Sunday, with Ohio State potentially falling out of the top 25 entirely.
body: One read of Saturday's college football schedule suggested we might be in for a sleepy weekend. After all, Week 12 marked the first time since 2009 that there were no games between teams ranked in the AP Top 25 poll (excluding 2020). Some differences with the College Football Playoff rankings did have one such game highlighted on the slate, but the lack of ranked-on-ranked matchups did stand in contrast to some of the seemingly loaded slates in previous weeks.
So of course it was Week 12, the week that had some of the least games between ranked teams, that provided one of the biggest shake-ups to the college football rankings we have seen this season.

The chaos came in the form of upsets, and the upset bug bit hard on the Big Ten. The conference had five teams in the AP poll last week but saw three of them lose on the road to unranked opponents. Seeing UCLA, Indiana and Ohio State all fall on the same day changed the math for the Big Ten title race and the College Football Playoff picture. We will find out what the selection committee has to say on Tuesday night, but the AP voters could give us a hint as to where all three will land after their projected drops in the rankings.

Ohio State may find itself all the way out of the top 25 entirely, which would mark the first time since 2011 that the Buckeyes would be unranked in the AP Top 25 poll (excluding 2020). Falling to No. 16 set Ohio State dangerously close to their previous AP poll low of No. 21, which is where the 2014 team bottomed out before charging back into the CFP picture and eventually winning the national title. Unfortunately, no such path is still available to Ryan Day's squad in 2026, as Ohio State enters its rivalry game against Michigan with a 7-4 record and very little momentum, having lost three of their last four games.

Trying to sort out the conference title tiebreakers and College Football Playoff conundrums will continue through the week, but after the chaos of Week 12, here's how we think the new AP Top 25 poll will look on Sunday:

1. Georgia (Last week -- 1): A spot in the final SEC Championship Game was clinched on Saturday as Georgia passed its final road test with a win at South Carolina. The Bulldogs were clinical in the 34-6 win, dominating on defense and leaning on the Gamecocks over four quarters to secure a fourth-straight double-digit win.
2. Utah (2): The Utes are currently in action at TCU.

3. Notre Dame (3): On a night when upsets and upset scares littered the top 25 scoreboard, Notre Dame was able to fly under the radar with a business-like approach to winning against SMU to improve to 10-1.
4. Miami (5): The Hurricanes trailed by two touchdowns early against Virginia Tech but stormed back to hold on for a 28-20 win that clinched their spot in the ACC Championship Game.

5. Tennessee (9): We are projecting a decent jump for Tennessee in the wake of its 27-13 win against LSU. The Vols were underdogs in the eyes of the oddsmakers against the unranked Tigers, but out-executed Lane Kiffin's group before a rocking atmosphere in Neyland Stadium. With a 9-2 record and another strong win, we're projecting AP voters will respect the head-to-head result against Alabama as they re-shuffle the top 10 following Saturday's chaos.

6. Alabama (7): The Crimson Tide rolled in their game against FCS Chattanooga, getting to rest Keelon Russell while also running up the score for the home fans. Backup quarterback Austin Mack totaled five touchdowns in relief (four passing, one rushing), and Alabama improved to 9-2 after the 47-0 win.

7. Texas (8): It was a great day for a boring blowout win, as Texas fans had limited anxiety during a stressful Saturday for other top-10 teams. The Longhorns led 24-3 at halftime and cruised to a 45-3 win that was highlighted by three total touchdowns from Arch Manning (two passing, one rushing) and noticeable skill position depth for Steve Sarkisian's offense.

8. Wake Forest (10): In a season that has been chaotic and unpredictable compared to weekly expectations, nothing has proven to be more consistent over the last month than Wake Forest. The Demon Deacons are smashing teams in the first half and cruising to double-digit wins against ACC opponents, continuing that trend on Saturday in a 50-29 win at Georgia Tech.

9. Texas Tech (11): The Red Raiders' defense answered the call on the road against in-state foe Baylor, holding the Bears to just 257 yards of offense at 3.62 yards per play. That edge was crucial to overcome three turnovers on offense and helped Texas Tech hold on for a 20-10 win to improve to 10-1 on the year.

10. UCLA (4): There is a value of aesthetics when it comes to how voters react to UCLA's first loss of the season. The Bruins were slow to make their move up in the rankings until they toppled Oregon, and even last week was ranked behind two other teams with losses despite having a 10-0 record. So yes, the AP voters might have some doubts that will be addressed in their re-ranking of UCLA following the upset loss.

11. BYU (12): The magic of Bear Bachmeier in the short areas proved to be enough for BYU to avoid a misstep on the road and keep their College Football Playoff argument strong. Bachmeier ran for two touchdowns, and Jojo Phillips pulled in the game-winning two-point try in triple overtime, breaking the hearts of the upset-minded Kansas fans in Lawrence.

12. Indiana (6): The Hoosiers are in some real trouble as injuries and close-game fortune have both seemingly turned the other way on the reigning national champions. Curt Cignetti saw more injuries to key starters, even as Josh Hoover returned to the lineup, and Indiana is set to tumble in the rankings with a 9-2 profile that's heavy on win total and lighter on win quality.

13. Iowa (13): The Hawkeyes won their fourth game in a row, pulling away from Illinois in a 34-17 win to improve to 9-2 overall. Iowa might need some help to make the Big Ten title game, but a win next week against Nebraska could secure an awfully impressive 10-2 season to present to the selection committee at the end of the year.

14. Oregon (14): The Ducks deserve a lot of credit for being able to rally back from a midseason slump, as the team's recent momentum seemed to travel with the team to East Lansing for their Friday night spotlight. Oregon poured on the points late for a 45-7 final score that keeps the Ducks in the conversation as they enter the final week of the regular season with an 8-3 record and a shot at cracking the top 12.
15. Boise State (15): The Broncos are currently in action against San Diego State.

16. USC (18): Lincoln Riley led the Trojans to a 35-21 win against Maryland to close out the home schedule at the Coliseum and set up a colossal showdown with UCLA next week at the Rose Bowl. USC might not have the exact Big Ten title or College Football Playoff stakes they wanted coming into the year, but the Trojans will be a main character in the final week of conference play for both competitions, and Riley has a chance to score a big win with the fans playing spoiler to the cross-town rivals.
17. Arizona (19): The Wildcats are currently in action at Kansas State.

18. Houston (20): We do not expect Houston to get docked for winning close, 34-31 at West Virginia, but the Cougars' resume strength isn't fantastic when voters are breaking ties on their ballots. Houston is 8-3 but 0-2 against other ranked teams (Utah, Texas Tech), with a top-35 caliber win against Oklahoma State as the highlight of the profile.

19. Louisville (21): Jeff Brohm is in position to finish the season somewhere close to the preseason expectations, with an 8-3 record heading into the rivalry game against Kentucky. Now, how Louisville has arrived at 8-3, with losses in two of the first three ACC games, was not expected. But after a win against Pitt, the Cardinals hold a solid top 25 resume with a chance to bolster that position against Will Stein net weekend in Lexington.

20. Liberty (22): The Flames were not ranked by the College Football Playoff Selection Committee but did crash the AP voters' top 25 last week. Now at 10-1 after a 45-14 home win against Western Kentucky, Liberty rides the power of that impressive winning percentage to a slight bump up.

21. Florida (23): The Gators did not offer a ton of evidence for continued voter support in a back-and-forth with Vanderbilt that saw both offenses move the ball effectively. Florida finished strong with a score and a fourth-down stop late in the fourth quarter, holding on for a 34-27 win.

22. Oklahoma (NR): A three-touchdown win against Texas A&M should propel the Sooners out of the "Others receiving votes" category and into the top 25. A head-to-head advantage against Ole Miss should help voters place Oklahoma on their ballots who might have had them off last week, since both teams are now 7-4 and the Sooners now have more SEC wins on the season.

23. Ole Miss (25): The margins were very thin at the cut line for the top 25, with Ole Miss holding the narrowest edge on the teams checking in at No. 26 and No. 27 in voting points. A 59-17 win against FCS Wofford doesn't boost their stock, but losses elsewhere should sharpen the ballot and have Ole Miss safely in the top 25 again.

24. Nebraska (NR): The quality loss Cornhuskers argue a four-loss team worth top 25 consideration after toppling Ohio State on Saturday in Lincoln. Matt Rhule's elusive win against a ranked team reverses the recent trend after close losses to Indiana, Oregon and Washington (by a combined 13 points) had Nebraska underperforming its quality in the conference standings. The entire resume doesn't offer a top of high-end wins aside from Saturday's win against the Buckeyes, but a recency bias could be enough to push Nebraska back into the top 25.

25. Missouri (NR): Welcome back, Missouri, to your spot here in the 20s of the AP Top 25 poll. The Tigers beat Kentucky on Saturday night, bouncing the Wildcats from the rankings and jumping ahead in line among those power conference teams on the cut line of the ballot. Missouri is 7-4 overall with a win against Florida to pair with the Week 12 win against the Wildcats, and if asked to choose between that resume and a two-loss Group of Six team, we project that the strength of schedule edge will win out in the eyes of the AP voters.
Projected to drop out: No. 16 Ohio State, No. 17 Kentucky, No. 24 Memphis

articles.headline: No. 3 Louisville women use 26-0 run to ease past Alaska Anchorage 113-40 in Great Alaska Shootout
keyFacts: No. 3 Louisville defeated Alaska Anchorage 113-40 in the Great Alaska Shootout on Saturday.
Louisville secured the win by scoring 26 unanswered points during the third quarter.
Louisville will play Seattle U for the tournament championship on Sunday.
body: ANCHORAGE, Alaska (AP) — Elif Istanbulluoglu scored 19 points, Imari Berry had 13 of her 16 in the first quarter, and No. 3 Louisville used a big third-quarter run to ease past Alaska Anchorage 113-40 on Saturday night in the Great Alaska Shootout.

Berry, who scored 20-plus in her last three games, had three 3-pointers in the opening six minutes and 13 of Louisville’s opening 24 points. The Cardinals led 34-14 after 10 minutes and extended it to 57-24 at halftime.

Louisville scored the opening seven points of the third to make it 64-24. After an Alaska Anchorage 3-pointer with 8:21 left in the frame, the Cardinals scored the next 26 points to go ahead 90-27. The Seawolves went nearly seven minutes without scoring.
A 5-0 run to begin the fourth made it 97-32 and Louisville reached the century mark with 7:08 to go.

Mackenly Randolph finished with 12 points and 10 rebounds, and junior Zamareya Jones had 11 points and a career-high 12 assists for her first career double-double for Louisville (8-0). Carys Baker scored 12 points off the bench and Tajianna Roberts added 10 points to reach double figures in the seventh game she's played in this season.
Amber Kartchner scored 11 points for Alaska Anchorage, which turned it over 20 times. The Seawolves were also outrebounded 51-18.
Louisville made a season-high 15 3-pointers on just 29 attempts, while Alaska Anchorage shot 15 of 53 overall.
Louisville also participated in the Great Alaska Shootout in 1999, going 1-1 with a win over Alaska Anchorage and a loss to Kansas.
Up next
The tournament continues on Sunday with Louisville playing Seattle U for the championship and Alaska Anchorage hosting Chicago State.

articles.headline: 'He will see what Man Utd are made of' - Pulis on Pochettino's first game
keyFacts: Mauricio Pochettino faces his first match as Manchester United manager against Liverpool this Sunday.
Former manager Tony Pulis says Pochettino will have limited time to prepare his squad for the upcoming game.
Pulis suggests Pochettino must gain control over future player recruitment to achieve long-term success at Manchester United.
body: - Published
Stepping into a job like Mauricio Pochettino has done at Manchester United, where managers have come and gone frequently, will always lead you to wonder why the others have not lasted very long.
Irrespective of results, you face these first few days in your new post with suspicion.
So, while what happens in Pochettino's first game against Liverpool on Sunday is important, it will not define his early opinions of the club - good or bad.
Whenever you take over a team in mid-season, which I did on a few occasions, you don't usually get much time to work with your players before your first game.

Jumping straight in and going straight to the heart of a two-day preparation for a game, like Pochettino has done before United go to Anfield, is so difficult and I am not sure any manager can honestly make a profound difference.

A change of voice helps, I'm sure, but so does showing strength and confidence in your own principles and making sure the players understand you demand complete and utter commitment in all the games you face, starting with this one.

With time on the training ground being so limited, my initial work would focus on us being a team and working up and down the pitch together, by breaking down different scenarios inside the game and what we should do in them.
I'd keep the focus on hard work and making us difficult to beat - clean sheets are so under-rated.
Then, on the day, your first pre-match speech is always a massive one, and it will be the same for Pochettino too.

My first team talk would always focus on generating an 'us against the world' mentality. As a manager coming in now, you've usually got the job because the team has struggled, so you can play on that to motivate the players.

You can use media reports and stories to show the negativity against them - but then counter that by producing a real 'stand-up and be counted' kind of rallying call, before sending them out on the pitch, while mentioning your faith in them to succeed.
'What your own eyes tell you is most important'
I would have selected my team before I met the players, through my own knowledge and also with help from within.

Whichever club I went in at, I'd expect to know something about most of the players within the group in terms of their position and ability, but understanding the character of the squad was vital too.

The existing staff would know more about the lads' qualities in that respect than myself or anyone who had just arrived with me, so I'd always discuss that with the people I had inherited, from fitness coaches to the medical department.

It's what your own eyes tell you that is most important, however. Going into your first game gives you the opportunity to see for yourself what your players are made of - and it can be a completely different view from what other people see.
Most of the early games I managed would be hit and miss in terms of selection, but I would quickly work out the strengths and weaknesses of the group.
As I've mentioned in previous columns, one of my first aims at any club where I was manager was about putting out a team, not a group of individuals.
It does not take long to see when that is not happening. I can remember my first game of my first spell at Stoke, a 4-2 defeat at Walsall in the Championship.

I wasn't universally enamoured by certain crowd favourites in that team and, while any manager knows that leaving some of them out could have an adverse effect on the supporters' view of yourself, you have to stand up and make decisions based on what you see.
It is the same if there are other issues with the squad you have inherited too.
West Brom's first game after I was appointed manager was a draw with West Ham on New Year's Day 2015.
I sat in the stands at Upton Park with my son, Anthony, who was concerned how different the Albion team was compared to Crystal Palace, the last team I had managed in the Premier League.
He was right to worry about it, but we still found a way - a totally different way of playing, but still a way to win that suited the group.
All your staff have to understand your objectives
My initial aims after arriving at any club mid-season were pretty direct and also pretty basic too.
The staff I inherited did not just know the players, they were also the first group who had to understand my objectives and also my principles - like the work ethic I expected, for example.
Irrespective of what they were used to doing, it was imperative they followed my lead.
One of the clubs I arrived at were struggling at the foot of the table and also suffering from a glut of injuries.
In my opinion, the players were taking advantage of a very honest and hard-working medical department, who were quite accommodating on the treatment times for the lads.
I changed that immediately, so injured players were treated at 9am, 2pm and 4pm, with sessions in-between those times for strength and recovery workouts.

This did not go down well with the players because it impeded on their social lives and, in one case, a player whose injury record was not exactly brilliant came to me complaining that his wife expected him to pick his children up from school and being asked to be in at 4pm affected his private life too.
I did not budge, and funnily enough the player in question recovered quite quickly - as did the majority of the other injured players.
'Clear the treatment rooms, and make sure the players are fit'

Asking injured players to be at the training ground all day was by far the best way of getting them fit, in my experience, and the medical departments I managed were all working well past 4pm anyway so it was no hardship to them.
Just on that side of things, I would sometimes get the feeling some medical departments thought that, if they weren't treating players, then they weren't doing their jobs.
That was completely the opposite to how I saw it. I would congratulate people for having empty treatment rooms and applaud them for their work.

Treatment rooms are comfort areas that certain players would always gravitate to, to have a kiss and a cuddle if they are feeling sorry for themselves for not being in the team. That's one of the first things that has to change, because you cannot give your players any excuses or hiding places if they are not performing.
Similarly, I have always laughed at new managers who take over in mid-season and complain about the lack of fitness in their squad.
I am sure I have done it myself at some point, but then I had a reputation of managing extremely fit squads of players and it was always an area I studied really closely.

Early on in my management career, we weren't blessed with the advanced fitness equipment used in football today, but I was still able to quickly arrive at the level I believed the players should be at.
How? Simple.
Firstly, I had my own fitness runs that were tried and tested but, also, I knew that if during a fitness session they weren't moaning and sweating, they weren't working hard enough.
Privately, you can realise very quickly when and which additions to the squad are needed.
Pochettino will no doubt be thinking about that at United already, but he has 10 games in the Premier League and Champions League before the January transfer window opens.
In the meantime, everything has to be geared towards winning games. I always knew I needed to do that quickly, because it helps the players believe in what I was doing, which is important too.
I've outlined my principles I held at every club above, and they never changed, but my playing principles were determined by the quality of the group I inherited.
My big strength as a coach was relaying what I needed from every individual player in the team, and I'm afraid repeated sessions were the go-to remedy to get there.

I apologise to all the lads who had to put up with me barking out the same commands, day after day, until even our weaker links would remember their individual and the team's plays in and out of possession.
'Bounce or not, future recruitment is key'
It goes without saying that with United changing their manager again, their supporters will be hoping for an immediate bounce in respect of results and performance.

Michael Carrick's results when he took the reins at Old Trafford at the start of this year were fantastic, with six wins and a draw in his first seven league games - including victories over Manchester City and Arsenal.
As a consequence, he steered United from mid-table to third place and Champions League qualification.
Even if Pochettino delivers something similar then, for that success to last, he has to be able to have more control over the future recruitment into the club.
That has been an absolute disaster recently, and I don't believe blame for it can be thrown in Carrick's direction.
In fact, Pochettino should use what has happened as his argument for what needs to change to achieve his aims of bringing United out of recession and on the road to recovery.
Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

articles.headline: Max Verstappen wins Las Vegas Grand Prix: Formula One 2026 – as it happened
keyFacts: Max Verstappen won the Las Vegas Grand Prix after a highly competitive race featuring multiple lead changes.
Oscar Piastri secured a podium finish after starting the race in 17th position.
The victory increased Max Verstappen's lead over George Russell in the Formula One drivers' championship.
body: For the round-up of what was frankly one of the best Formula 1 races in years, my colleague Giles Richards had the privilege of watching live from Vegas.
You can read his full report here:
Thanks for following along our live blog today. It was a day of some serious racing, and I reckon it’ll be remembered for a while yet.
As mentioned, Carlos Sainz took eighth spot from George Russell right at the end.
Liam Lawson who had started right at the back of the pack finished just a few places ahead in 15th. BUT he managed to clock the fastest lap of the race.
Unfortunately for him, while that used to give the driver an extra point, the FIA has since taken out that little bonus.
And of course I can’t go past the fact that Oscar Piastri started in 17th and ended up on the podium in a pretty heroic effort.
Mercedes will have some serious questions to answer

The race looked promising for the silver arrows who somehow squibbed it by the last lap with Kimi Antonelli finishing in fourth behind the two McLarens and George Russell who had spent half the race battling for first – in ninth.
Russell even got pipped at the finish line by none other than Carlos Sainz Jr.
There will be some serious questions for the team to answer on how that went so wrong. It seems like there was some sort of power down turn or failure at the end.
No one can quite believe just how nuts that race was.

The win has further cemented Max Verstappen’s second place status in the drivers’ championship now an extra 23 points ahead of George Russell (I think puts him 40 points ahead but feel free to check my maths).
Verstappen is asked if he’s ever experienced a race quite like this before. Nup, he says:
Not in Formula One, that’s for sure. So yeah, crazy. I mean, really, really surreal and something that I’ve never seen before in in Formula One myself.
He also remarks on that crazy slip stream advantage, and the call to his team asking for some strategy support:

I think in the beginning we had the deployment immediately correct, but of course people are learning and watching what you’re doing. And at one point I couldn’t get back into the lead before the start finish line, so that’s why I asked the question.

I think we had it set up well, and it was yeah just crazy amount of fighting and the the slipstream was so big that yeah you you it was just impossible to drive off and it was just crazy how many people were just following.
Keanu Reeves chauffeurs the podium winners to the Bellagio for the ceremony
What. A. Race!
That was an absolute privilege to watch and blog for you!
Our top three drivers today are being chauffeured to the Bellagio hotel now for the podium ceremony by none other than actor Keanu Reeves! What can’t that man do?
Verstappen is told by his team that he’s already deploying the best strategy they have so there’s nothing left in the tool box. In the final lap the cars can deplete their entire battery though.
Oscar Piastri has inched ahead of Lando Norris into fourth spot.
This is going to be a real nail-biting finish. It’s a two way race between Max Verstappen and Kimi Antonelli in first and second.

The silver arrows has the advantage on the final straight, and over the last few laps, Verstappen has been desperately trying to claw back the lead just before that finish line. It’s about 50/50 at the moment on whether he can get the lead before or after the line.
At the back of the Grid, Isack Hadjar has jumped from 19th to 15th. That’s not really saying a whole lot though, he’s overtaken the remaining Cadillac, the two Aston Martins and Liam Lawson.
Charles Leclerc gets a ten second penalty for the clash with Lewis Hamilton. That’s the second penalty for Ferrari this race.
Meanwhile Kimi Antonelli uses Max Verstappen’s slip stream on the straight and slides into the lead.
But how long can he hold it? Just enough that if this was the last lap, he would have won, but by turn one Verstappen’s got it back. It’s going to be TIGHT.
Max Verstappen tests out his hypothesis with Antonelli getting in front, but Verstappen is just able to nose in front by what would be the finish line. So he might still be able to clinch that win.
Verstappen has figured out that his weak spot is turn 14 where the Mercedes overtake, and he’s only able to get it back by turn one of the following lap.
That’s bad news for him, if Russell or Antonelli inch ahead on the final lap leaving Verstappen with no room to fight back. He gives the warning to his team on the radio.
While the Ferrari battle has taken both drivers back down the grid, Kimi Antonelli has overtaken his teammate George Russell without drama and immediately sets his sights on Verstappen.
He takes him on, gets in front but Verstappen again reclaims the lead on turn one.
Things are not looking good for the Ferraris with the two touching, sending Hamilton back into tenth and Leclerc into eight. They get overtaken by Franco Colapinto.
Sounds like they need some serious conversations about teamwork.
George Russell, is trying AGAIN for first, struggles, and then gets overtaken by Lando Norris who takes advantage of the fight between the Mercedes and Red Bull.
Norris holds second and then takes the lead!!!
Unfortunately the McLaren kind of sucks on the straight and Verstappen takes back the lead.
It’s now 1 Verstappen, 2 Norris, 3 Russell, and then Piastri in fourth.
Feels like deja vu at this point. George Russell briefly gets in front, but at turn three, Max Verstappen takes the inside line and get the lead back with relative ease.
The stewards say they’ll be investigating some sort of incident between Russell and Isack Hadjar earlier in the race, about half an hour ago. We’ll keep you updated on that.
Norris tries again to get in front of Pierre Gasly but still can’t best the Frenchman.
Lewis Hamilton, sitting in eight spot has clocked fastest lap. He’s just 0.4 behind Oscar Piastri who’s just half a second behind Ferrari teammate Charles Leclerc.
As I said, they’re all damn close, and they’re all using the slip streams!

Isack Hadjar is back on the track, and has switched back to soft tyres along with getting a new front wing, those should last him to the end of the race, and will give him a little extra speed while most of the other drivers are on mediums.
The McLarens are moving their way up slowly and taking advantage, Lando Norris has just gone past Pierre Gasly into P3, with Oscar Piastri back to where he was before the pit stop in eight.
That didn’t last long, Norris is back into fourth with Gasly claiming back the podium place.
Part of Isack Hadjar’s front wing has just disintegrated! He’s tumbling down the grid to 13th already, losing so much time. There’s a bunch of debris on the track from the car.
On the radio, Red Bull tells Hadjar to box this lap to get it fixed. He’ll really struggle to get back to the front of the pack with a second pit stop.
We’re back to normal racing. Liam Lawson might just have the warmest tyres with the softs having used the safety car to catch up from far back – he’s in 19th.
Antonelli, Bearman, Bottas, Camara and Lawson are on soft tyres.
The Perez / Camara clash is being investigated. Perez is already out of the race, but we’ll see whether any penatlies are dished out.
The camera catches Arvid Lindblad walking off, he’s looking pretty disappointed after what was a strong race for him. His tyres were just too cold leading to the spin out.
Lindblad isn’t yet 21 so can’t even hit the bar for a consolation drink.
The cars are driving so close to each other tonight with the gigantic slip stream advantage on the course.
There are now three drivers out of the race: Arvid Lindblad who spun out after a pit stop, Sergio Perez who just crashed into the wall (what’s new for the Cadillacs) and Alex Albon who never started.
Hamilton says he didn’t have any other option but to go off the track when he overtook Norris, but the problem was that he completed the overtake after he did it.
There’s precedence for the penalty. Doesn’t make it any easier.

articles.headline: Dozens missing as deadly fire hits Indonesian candy factory
keyFacts: At least three people died and four were injured in a fire at an Indonesian candy factory, officials said.
Rescue teams are searching for 36 missing workers out of 60 people inside the factory, officials said.
Joint rescue teams are making maximum effort to locate the victims while prioritizing safety, an official said.
body: Indonesian rescue teams are searching for 36 workers who remained unaccounted for after a fire at a candy-making factory killed at least three people, officials said on Sunday.
The fire occurred at the Fonusa Agung Mulia factory, around 50 kilometers (31 miles) west of the capital, Jakarta, in the Serang district of Banten province.
What do we know about the Indonesian confectionery factory fire?
The factory caught fire on Saturday afternoon, local search and rescue agency official Rizky Dwianto said.
"All elements of the joint SAR (search-and-rescue) team are making maximum effort to locate the victims while prioritizing the safety of personnel in the field," he added.
Rizky said four people injured in the blaze had been taken to a nearby hospital and health clinic. Eleven more were said to have been rescued alive.
The governor of Banten province, Andra Soni, told reporters overnight that 60 people were believed to have been inside the factory when the fire broke out.
Drone footage shows the fire destroyed large sections of the three-story building, bringing down the roof in some places.
Survivors said the fire started in a cooling unit on the third floor.
The factory produces Milkita, an Indonesian brand of milk-based candies and snack products.
Deadly industrial fires in Indonesia
Indonesia has seen a series of deadly industrial fires in recent years, raising questions about the country's workplace safety standards into question.
Among other disasters, at least 22 people were killed in a fire last December that broke out in a seven-story building in Jakarta after a suspected drone battery explosion, police said.
An explosion in a nickel-processing plant in the east of the country killed at least 13 people in 2023.

articles.headline: Trump says Sen. John Cornyn is doing a ‘tremendous disservice’ by blocking Texas judicial pick
keyFacts: President Trump said Senator John Cornyn is doing a disservice by blocking judicial nominee T. Elliot Gaiser for a Dallas court seat.
Cornyn said Trump nominated a non-Texan without consultation and urged the president to consider an alternative candidate.
Senator Ted Cruz said Cornyn's refusal to sign a blue slip leaves the seat vacant, allowing Democrats to fill it.
body: Trump says Sen. John Cornyn is doing a ‘tremendous disservice’ by blocking Texas judicial pick
By
Greg Norman-Diamond, Fox News
Published Nov. 22, 2026, 12:56 a.m. ET
See more of our coverage in your search results.
President Trump told Fox News’ “Saturday in America” that outgoing Texas Sen. John Cornyn is doing a “tremendous disservice” by blocking his pick to fill a judicial seat in Dallas.
“We’re going to have a radical left lunatic get in there, and we don’t want that,” the president said.

Trump’s comments come after Cornyn told The Associated Press he has no intention of returning the “blue slip” for T. Elliot Gaiser, a Department of Justice senior lawyer who was nominated by the president to the US District Court for the Northern District of Texas.
Advertisement
The blue slip tradition allows for home state senators to weigh in on judicial nominees, giving them a say on who does and doesn’t move forward.
Returning a blue slip is the equivalent of giving a thumbs up to the nominees moving forward, while keeping the slip effectively blocks the process.

“Everybody tells me he’s outstanding, and he’s being held up by John Cornyn because John Cornyn’s feelings were hurt,” said Trump, who endorsed Cornyn’s challenger, Ken Paxton, in the Texas Republican Senate primary.
Advertisement

“And, by the way, John Cornyn would have lost. It was just a point in time. John Cornyn would have lost by a lot. You know, one of those things. But he was beaten in the primary. And he’s. He feels badly about it,” the president continued.
“He’s a nice guy, John Cornyn, but he’s doing a tremendous disservice because Gaiser is fantastic.”
Cornyn wrote on X later Saturday, “If President Trump wanted to fill a judicial vacancy in Dallas, why did he wait until after the midterms to nominate someone?”
Advertisement

“The seat has been vacant since 2025. Then, without any consultation, he nominates a non-Texan with little connection to the Lone Star State, with no trial court experience and who has not been appropriately vetted for a lifetime job. The Senate has a constitutional responsibility to provide ‘advice and consent,’ which is impossible without consultation,” Cornyn added.

“Still, I would like to work with the President to fill the seat while we still have a Senate majority. I have forwarded an outstanding candidate who was highly rated by Senator Cruz’s and my bipartisan Federal Judicial Evaluation Committee, and who has now been interviewed by White House Counsel.
“All that is needed is an FBI background check (which) they stand ready to do on a timely basis,” Cornyn also said. “Back to you, Mr. President. Time is of the essence.”
Advertisement
Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, called Cornyn’s move “really frustrating,” describing to Fox News’ “Saturday in America” a tense encounter he had with Cornyn this week in Washington.

“I came to him on the Senate floor, and I asked him to please let this judge go. And I tried to make the case on the merits that he’d make a fantastic judge. And I asked him, ‘Will you just meet with him?’ Because Cornyn refused even to meet with him,” Cruz said.

“He wouldn’t talk to him. He just said, ‘No, no, no.’ And I was asking him, I said, ‘Look, you’re going to give this seat to the Democrats. Why would you want to do that?’ And, unfortunately, he got very angry. He began screaming. He began cursing at me,” Cruz added.
Advertisement

Cruz said, after the Republican losses in the midterm elections, “All the Republicans agreed, ‘Let’s do everything humanly possible to confirm every judge we can before the end of the year, because we know the Democrats are going to come in January,’ and I expect they’re going to block all judicial confirmations.”

“We had two vacancies in Texas, one in Austin that we’re moving forward with. And we’ll have that judge confirmed by the end of the year. We had a second vacancy in Dallas, and the problem was that we did not have time to have a brand-new nominee go through the paperwork, the FBI background check,” Cruz told Fox News.

“That takes weeks and weeks and weeks, and we simply didn’t have time between now and the end of the year to get that done. And, so, the White House proposed a different idea, which is to go with a senior lawyer at the Department of Justice, a man named Elliot Gaiser, an incredibly qualified judicial nominee.
“This is someone who was a law clerk at the U.S. Supreme Court for Justice Sam Alito. He was a state solicitor general arguing cases before the United States Supreme Court,” Cruz said.
Advertisement
“And he’s right now the head of the Office of Legal Counsel, which is the senior constitutional advisor to the president and the senior constitutional advisor to the attorney general.”
Cruz also told Fox News he interviewed Gaiser and called him “incredibly principled, smart, capable, ready.”

Cruz added that Gaiser “was a fantastic nomination. I was enthusiastic. Unfortunately, my colleague John Cornyn decided to block the nomination, and any one senator can block a district court nomination from your state.
Advertisement

“And, so, Cornyn did what’s called — he refused to return the blue slip, which basically means he vetoed it — and the result of that is the seat is going to remain vacant. The people of Dallas are not going to have a judge in that seat. And he basically gave the seat to the Democrats,” Cruz said.

articles.headline: Kenya’s internet metering bill raises privacy and affordability concerns
keyFacts: Kenya’s proposed internet metering bill, sponsored by MP Marianne Jebet Kitany, would require providers to monitor subscribers and introduce identifiable meter numbers.
The Communications Authority, telecommunications companies, and civil society groups have raised concerns about data privacy, affordability, and increased compliance costs.
The National Assembly’s Departmental Committee is currently considering the legislation while opponents urge lawmakers to reject compulsory metering in favor of alternative consumer safeguards.
body: Nairobi, Kenya – A proposed law requiring internet service providers in Kenya to monitor subscribers’ data consumption and introduce identifiable meter numbers has drawn opposition from industry and civil society groups, amid concerns about affordability, privacy and the handling of personal information.

The Kenya Information and Communications (Amendment) Bill, 2025, sponsored by Aldai MP Marianne Jebet Kitany, seeks to make consumption-based internet billing mandatory. It would require providers to assign each customer a unique meter number, monitor usage, convert it into readable details and issue invoices based on consumption.

The Bill’s stated objective is to protect consumers from unfair billing and ensure they pay for the internet they use. But the Communications Authority of Kenya (CA), telecommunications companies and civil society organisations have questioned whether mandatory metering is necessary and whether the proposed framework provides adequate safeguards for subscribers’ information.

The debate has intensified as the National Assembly’s Departmental Committee on Communication, Information and Innovation considers the legislation. The regulator has urged legislators not to make metered billing compulsory, while Telkom Kenya has warned of potential consequences for privacy, affordability and investment.
Privacy at risk

The Bill would require internet service providers to operate systems that monitor customer usage, convert consumption into readable details and generate invoices. Providers would also have to submit information about their billing systems, including subscriber meter numbers, to the regulator at least once every financial year.

The proposed provisions do not expressly require providers to record the content of private messages or the websites subscribers visit. However, civil society organisations have questioned what usage information would be collected and how identifiable records would be stored, accessed and shared.

The International Commission of Jurists (ICJ) Kenya has questioned the necessity of mandatory metering, arguing that the regulator already has powers to address billing complaints and protect consumers.

Demas Kiprono of ICJ Kenya has argued that the proposed system raises questions about whether the collection of identifiable usage information is necessary and proportionate to the Bill’s stated consumer-protection objective.

The concerns relate to the potential consequences of linking individual subscribers to records of their internet use. Critics say the legislation should specify who could access such information, how long it could be retained and the circumstances in which it could be disclosed.

Kenya’s Data Protection Act, 2019, already provides a framework for processing personal information. Opponents of the Bill say Parliament should make clear how those protections would apply to the proposed metering system.
The Mokaya case
Questions about telecommunications data have also featured in court proceedings involving university student David Ooga Mokaya.

He was arrested in November 2024 over a social media post concerning President William Ruto and charged with publishing false information. On February 19 this year, Senior Principal Magistrate Caroline Nyaguthii acquitted him under Section 215 of the Criminal Procedure Code, finding that the prosecution had not proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.

After his acquittal, Mokaya filed a petition at the High Court seeking protection of his personal information. He argued that information, including call data records, subscriber details, location data and metadata had been supplied to investigators without his consent. The allegations form part of the separate civil proceedings and should not be treated as a final judicial finding.

On February 25, Justice Bahati Mwamuye issued interim conservatory orders restraining the respondents and interested parties from transferring, sharing or disclosing Mokaya’s personal data without his written consent, a valid court order or an express provision of written law permitting disclosure.

The orders were issued pending further proceedings in the case. They do not establish that the proposed internet metering system would be used for surveillance. They do, however, illustrate the legal questions that can arise over the collection and disclosure of telecoms data.
The cost of data
Privacy is not the only concern. Mandatory consumption-based billing could also affect how households and businesses budget for connectivity.

In a submission to parliament on November 3, the Communications Authority cautioned against making metered billing compulsory across the sector. It said the approach could have unintended consequences for affordability, digital inclusion and consumer choice, particularly among low-income households, students, small businesses and communities in underserved areas.
The regulator noted that background applications, software updates, streaming and cloud services can consume data without users closely monitoring their usage.

Instead of prescribing one billing model, the Authority proposed usage alerts when subscribers reach 50, 80 and 100 percent of their data allowance, free real-time usage dashboards and monthly spending caps. It also recommended independent certification and periodic audits of metering systems, clearer itemised bills and stronger procedures for resolving billing disputes.
The Authority’s position is that consumer protection can be strengthened through regulations and licensing requirements without requiring every provider to adopt consumption-based pricing.

The financial impact of a change would depend on providers’ pricing and individual patterns of internet use. Customers who consume relatively little data could benefit from paying according to usage, while those who rely on large or continuous data allowances could face different costs. The Bill does not set the retail prices providers would charge.
Business concerns
Telecommunications companies have questioned whether the proposed changes could impose additional costs on providers and affect investment in broadband services.

Telkom Kenya Chief Executive Officer Mugo Kibati told the parliamentary committee on November 10 that mobile internet accounts for about 96 percent of data subscriptions and is already billed by volume. The proposed changes would therefore mainly affect fixed broadband services, which account for the remaining share, he said.
According to the Kenya News Agency’s report of the hearing, Telkom argued that a uniform metering framework could increase compliance costs and create risks for subscriber privacy and investment.

The company proposed that providers disclose their billing models, charges and fair-use policies before customers subscribe. It also called for free access to consumption information, itemised bills on request, effective dispute-resolution mechanisms and independent audits where billing accuracy is questioned.

Telkom further urged legislators to protect unlimited and speed-based internet packages, allow providers at least 18 months to comply with any new requirements and require aggregated rather than individually identifiable subscriber information to be submitted to the regulator.

Carole Kairuki, chief executive of the Kenya Private Sector Alliance, also raised concerns about the potential effect of mandatory metering on businesses. In an interview with Al Jazeera, she said changes to internet billing could increase compliance costs and make connectivity expenses less predictable for businesses, particularly smaller enterprises.
A wider debate

The Bill’s memorandum says the proposed amendments are intended to protect consumers from exploitation and secure their economic interests under Article 46 of the Constitution. It also states that the legislation does not limit fundamental rights and freedoms.
The disagreement is over whether mandatory metering is the most effective way to achieve that objective and whether the proposed provisions offer sufficient protection for subscribers’ information.

The debate comes amid wider public scrutiny of digital rights and the handling of online activity in Kenya, particularly following the 2024 protests against the Finance Bill. Kelvin Kubai, an Advocate of the High Court of Kenya, told Al Jazeera that internet access is important to young people’s civic participation and their ability to hold public officials accountable. He argued that any new regulatory framework should take those uses into account.

Parliament must weigh the Bill’s consumer-protection objective against concerns raised by the regulator, internet providers and civil society groups. The Communications Authority has proposed greater billing transparency, usage alerts and independent audits as alternatives to compulsory consumption-based billing.
Telkom CEO Kibati warned politicians against imposing obligations that could undermine a developing sector.
“Sometimes you can go overboard in trying to protect consumers that you actually kill a nascent, growing sector,” he told the parliamentary committee.

articles.headline: New draft deal aims to avert collapse of talks at climate summit
keyFacts: UN COP31 climate summit negotiators are reviewing a new draft agreement after the original deadline passed without a deal.
The latest text acknowledges the world is on track to miss the 1.5C warming goal but omits specific language on transitioning away from fossil fuels.
Countries are scheduled to reconvene Sunday to vote on the deal, which could be suspended until next year if no consensus is reached.
body: - Published
Talks were set to resume at the UN COP31 summit on Sunday for a second day of overtime as countries struggled to reach a new global climate deal.
A new draft agreement was published in the early hours of Sunday which the Turkey and Australia co-hosts hoped would bridge the divide between nations.

Although it still includes no specific reference to "transitioning away from fossil fuels" - an omission in the previous draft that sparked threats of walkouts - it does acknowledge a previous commitment made by countries to do just that three years ago.
And it includes for the first time a recognition that the world is on track to miss the crucial goal of keeping temperatures below 1.5C of warming.
The EU and Pacific states had been arguing against the removal of fossil fuels from the draft text. The EU has not yet reacted to this latest draft.
The Africa Group is likely to be disappointed at this latest iteration as it includes no specific figure on money for adaptation and instead kicks that decision to future meetings.
Countries were expected to reconvene at 09:00 local time (06:00GMT) to decide whether to approve a new deal.

If countries cannot reach consensus - as required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended until next year. This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.
Just hours before the new text was published, EU Commissioner for Climate Wopke Hoekstra said if the bloc could not get "what is needed in terms of climate action... then there's no deal."
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, the UK's chief negotiator, struck a more hopeful tone, saying her team was still working to get an agreement.

A draft deal unveiled earlier this week called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels, but a second, pared-down version released on Thursday stripped away all mentions of coal, oil and gas - sparking threats of a walk out.

The fallout led to the summit in Antalya blowing past the original deadline of Friday. On Saturday negotiating teams who had Sunday morning flights were rescheduling them - a sign a deal was still not in sight, and raising the risk that as teams eventually had to leave, the meeting could lose the critical numbers needed to pass an agreement.

As part of a last ditch effort to produce an acceptable text, the European Union and Saudi Arabia - who were deeply divided over the future of fossil fuels - were brought together on Saturday to seek a compromise.
COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum told delegates in the early hours of Sunday he believed concerns had been addressed.
"We ask you to look at this decision carefully," Kurum said. "We are closer than ever to agreement on the remaining issues."
What has the issue been?

Ministers from Panama, Solomon Islands, Cote d'Ivoire and the EU were fighting to have a commitment to move away from fossil fuels put back into the final agreement, after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal.

"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.
Tuvalu's Climate Minister Maina Talia told reporters it was a "red line" for the low-lying Pacific nation: "We're talking about the root cause of all of this".

France's Minister of Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut, took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage (CCUS) - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.
"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.
In the latest text the commitments to CCUS have been reduced, which may be enough to alleviate the EU's concerns.

For the first time at a COP, the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - could acknowledge that the goal set under the Paris climate accord of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.
The world is entering a period called "overshoot".
Beyond this point scientists warn millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.
But Australia's Climate Change and Energy Minister, Chris Bowen, who is leading negotiations, pushed back on the need to include language on fossil fuels.
He argued the summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.
'We did not come here to beg'
One of the other key issues raised by developing nations - the lack of money - appears unresolved in the latest draft agreement.
Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn (Â£91bn) by 2035 - a figure that was then removed.

"We did not come here to beg, we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.
Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.
"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.

articles.headline: These Piranha Plant Slippers Double as Mario-themed Decor When You Put Them Away
keyFacts: Piranha Plant slippers feature a Pipe holder that allows the footwear to function as Super Mario-themed decor when not in use.
Amazon is offering the slippers for approximately $20 to Prime members as part of a Black Friday sale.
The slippers are available in only one size, designed to fit women's shoe sizes 6-9 or men's shoe sizes 5-8.
body: Slippers are one of those classic Christmas gifts pretty much everyone has received at some point in their lives. They are one of those practical items that everyone is going to use at some point, but rarely do people actually get excited when they unwrap a new pair of slippers. Sure, there are plenty of themed options out there that feel fun, but where do you even put those when you aren't using them?

Well, if it's a pair of Piranha Plant slippers, that problem has been solved for you. Just place them back in their Pipe holder and your footwear is instantly transformed into a little Piranha Plant. Suddenly you've got a fun piece of Super Mario-themed decor that brightens up the space.

The Piranha Plant slippers are getting discounted as part of Amazon's Black Friday sale , dropping the price down to about $20. The deal is only available for Amazon Prime Members, but the typical price is still pretty cheap as far as Nintendo-themed gifts go. They are sold by a third-party seller, but the Amazon reviews are overall quite positive.

The main thing to note before you buy these slippers is that there is only one size available. It's a bit hidden in the product listing, but the page states that they are designed to fit for women with a shoe size ranging from 6-9 or men's shoe size beween 5-8 in the US. So if you're someone with bigger feet, you're probably going to have trouble actually wearing these things around the house.

And while adults can certainly wear these, they seem like an ideal gift for kids. If they had these in my size I would absolutely grab a pair at this price. I would have loved getting these as a kid too, but I don't think these even existed when my feet were still that small. Still, I'm definitely considering picking up a pair for my nephew who has fairly recently discovered Mario games for the first time.
Looking for more Piranha Plant gifts? I recommend checking out the Piranha Plant Switch 2 Dock or the LEGO Super Mario Piranha Plant set .

articles.headline: Anthropic stock slides with rest of market after big-ticker IPO
keyFacts: Anthropic stock declined after its initial public offering on Thursday as part of a broader technology sell-off.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite closed more than 10% below their October highs on Friday following a turbulent week for the stock market.
Investors are weighing the technology sector's long-term viability amid expected interest rate hikes and recent political shifts in Congress.
body: The S&P 500 closed more than 10% below its October high on Friday alongside a similar drop in the technology-heavy Nasdaq Composite, ending a tumultuous week for a stock market largely reliant on the success of artificial intelligence companies.

Anthropic , one of the leading AI labs, went public on Thursday as the market continued reacting to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s recent resignation and Democrats retaking control of Congress in the 2026 midterm elections. After pricing its IPO at $83.00 per share, the company’s stock intially surged before sliding amid the broader technology sell-off to end the week.

The S&P notched its worst weekly performance since President Donald Trump announced widespread tariffs in April 2025. Investors weighing the sector’s long-term viability widely expect a 25-basis-point rate hike in December and have long been wary of a possible correction following months of stock market highs. The correction comes not long after a midterm election cycle in which voters concerned about data center construction and AI’s impacts on the job market forced lawmakers to reckon with the emerging technology and its impact on constituents.

Gov. Greg Abbott (R-TX) and Gov. Josh Shapiro (D-PA) both took steps to restrict data center development in August, before broader safety and cybersecurity concerns began dominating public discourse ahead of early November.
ANTHROPIC OPENS ON WALL STREET AFTER LARGEST IPO IN HISTORY

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and other industry titans such as Elon Musk and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have become key public figures throughout Trump’s second term in office. Trump has broadly backed policies meant to incentivize rather than stifle AI development, arguing the technology is beneficial to the country writ large and will lead to rapid economic growth.

Democrats took advantage of “affordability” concerns to retake control of both the House and the Senate earlier this month. 2028 presidential candidates will have to prove to voters they can pair AI policies with initiatives that curb inflation and address cost-of-living concerns.

articles.headline: 46 Years Later, the Most Influential Thriller of All Time Is Officially Free on YouTube
keyFacts: The 1980 horror film Friday the 13th is now available to watch for free on YouTube.
The film is considered influential for its realistic gore effects by Tom Savini and its unique choice of a mother as the primary killer.
The release coincides with the production of Crystal Lake, a new prequel series from A24 and Peacock.
body: Over the years, corporations and filmmakers alike have eagerly sought to revisit the origins of horror classics (e.g., Bates Motel and Psycho, Welcome to Derry and IT, etc.) for modern audiences. It’s an easy way to find successwhen you already have an audience that loves the IP you’re reimagining

Not even the Friday the 13th franchise has escaped the trend of revisiting the past. Crystal Lake, a new series from A24 and Peacock, follows Pamela Voorhees (Betsy Palmer), Jason Voorhees’s deranged mother. It’s a prequel that, frankly, nobody really asked for (though we kind of liked it anyway), since Jason’s origins have already been explored: Sean S. Cunningham’s 1980s horror film Friday the 13th — available to watch now for free on YouTube.
How Friday the 13th redefined a genre

Following the release of the genre-defining slasher Halloween, Cunningham and writer Victor Miller faced a real challenge: how to stand out in a subgenre flooded with horror movies (Black Christmas, Texas Chainsaw Massacre, to name just a few) trying to ride the slasher wave. Friday the 13th had to be memorable, interesting, and stand out.

On the surface, Friday the 13th doesn’t feel too different. It’s full of horny teens, heavy suspense, and a sense of isolation as a deranged killer hunts and kills them off, one by one. However, unlike other slashers like Halloween, Cunningham takes the brutality one step further by asking two very different but meaningful questions. Careful now, spoilers for a 46-year-old movie ahead.

First, what if the killer were not a man in a mask but a vengeful mother driven mad by society’s disregard for her disabled son? Second, what if Cunningham and Paramount hired Tom Savini, famous for his work on George A. Romero’s Dawn of the Dead, to create some of the most gruesome deaths audiences had yet seen on the silver screen?

The result is one of the bloodiest slashers of all time, one that shook up perceptions of how grotesque the horror subgenre could be and who, exactly, could be the one dealing out those kills in the first place.

Slashers like Halloween and Black Christmas have some gnarly kills—who could forget Michael Myers pinning Bob to a pantry door with a large knife or Barb being stabbed with a unicorn figurine’s horn? Savini, however, elevated Friday the 13th’s kills into a bloody art form with shocking, realistic gore.

Savini did more than deliver, too. Just as he used practical effects for Dawn of the Dead, he did so again for several of the film’s kills. One especially memorable kill is counselor Jack’s, in which he’s stabbed in the neck as he lies in bed. Using a prosthetic neck piece and a pump, fake blood was pumped to create a blood-spurt effect that, for its time, looked remarkably realistic.

The most significant thing that set Friday the 13th apart from its predecessors, however, was its killer: Pamela Voorhees. The slasher genre was no longer defined by masculine rage, but by a mother’s love. Even in the modern era of horror, slashers still feature far more male than female killers, but in 1980, Mrs. Voorhees was undoubtedly one of a kind.

Furthermore, for as deranged and murderous as she was, she exerted a strange, empathetic pull on audiences. Yes, murder is wrong — but you can’t deny that she loved her son. Unlike Michael Myers, who is often depicted as evil incarnate, Mrs. Voorhees has a complexity that made her brutal motives more compelling.

46 years later, Mrs. Voorhees's story begins anew with Crystal Lake. It’s unclear whether the series will get a second season, but even if it doesn’t, fans of Jason and his diabolical family tree needn’t worry. You can never go wrong with the original.
Friday the 13th is available to stream now for free on YouTube.

articles.headline: Astarion's Baldur's Gate 3 prequel novel infuriated fans, now it's Shadowheart's turn
keyFacts: Author Tasha Suri will write an official Baldur's Gate 3 prequel novel centered on the character Shadowheart.
The story follows Shadowheart investigating a murder mystery within the Church of Shar alongside other characters from the game.
The book is scheduled for release on June 8 in hardcover, ebook, and audiobook formats.
body: Tasha Suri, author of the Burning Kingdoms trilogy and several other books, will be writing Baldur's Gate 3: Shadowheart, the official BG3books website has announced. Another prequel to Larian's videogame, this one focuses on Shadowheart's time as a priestess in the Church of Shar, and is about a murder mystery.

"When a member of their order is killed in the Upper City," the blurb goes, "Shadowheart and her so-called allies are called to investigate. She trusts none of them: not Mirie, the ambitious Griefguard; not Caldan, the cynical propagandist; and certainly not Nocturne, the charming quartermistress, who claims to have only Shadowheart’s best interests in mind."

Mirie and Nocturne are both characters you can meet in Baldur's Gate 3, while Caldan Darkwood is mentioned in a note you can find. Nocturne in particular has a close relationship with Shadowheart, which could be interesting to see developed. "Torn between the familiar comforts of the dark and the thrill of new desire," the blurb continues, "she must solve the mystery to prove her devotion… or be cast into the light."

Which sounds fine and dandy, but it'll have an uphill battle with the Baldur's Gate 3 fandom, who've been vocally critical of the Astarion novel for its lightness of tone—especially given his traumatic backstory—and apparently mischaracterizing Astarion and his sire, Cazador, as well as being inaccurate to the lore.

I haven't read the Astarion book, but I did read the original Baldur's Gate novels, which were terrible. So were almost all the D&D books I read in a youthful post-Tolkien haze where I'd put up with anything that had wizards in it. My expectations are pretty low, but I do like to slip a trashy fantasy novel between heavier reads as a palate-cleanser so maybe I'll try this one some day.

Baldur's Gate 3: Shadowheart will be out in a 304-page hardcover edition and in ebook form on June 8, as well as a 10-hour audiobook. The Astarion audiobook was read by Astarion performer Neil Newbon, we'll have to wait and see if Jennifer English reads the Shadowheart book.

If the series continues I could see a Wyll prequel being interesting, since he gets a bit short-changed in the videogame, though I wouldn't expect it to sell as well as novels about the more popular companions.
