articles.headline: 17 major federal agencies flagged over cybersecurity gaps as watchdog warns of increased attack risk
keyFacts: A Government Accountability Office report found 17 of 22 major federal agencies failed to fully implement required cybersecurity planning guidance.
The watchdog warned that these gaps in zero trust architecture increase the risk of cyberattacks and operational disruptions across government systems.
The GAO issued 40 recommendations to the agencies, and most departments agreed to develop or improve their cybersecurity strategies in response.
body: A sweeping federal watchdog report found that 17 of 22 major civilian agencies failed to fully address key cybersecurity planning guidance, warning that the shortcomings could leave government systems more vulnerable to cyberattacks and operational disruptions.

The Government Accountability Office (GAO) released its findings this week, identifying gaps at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Department of Justice ( DOJ ), Department of State , Department of the Treasury and Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), among others.

The report examined whether agencies had incorporated selected federal guidance into their plans for implementing zero trust architecture, a cybersecurity approach requiring users, devices and systems to be verified before accessing protected networks.
RETIRED FBI AGENT WARNS NCIC BREACH COULD THREATEN POLICE SAFETY DURING TRAFFIC STOPS
Only five of the 22 agencies fully addressed the selected guidance as of August 2026, prompting GAO to issue 40 recommendations to the remaining 17.
"Agencies would therefore be at increased risk of cyberattacks that could interrupt operations or otherwise compromise agency resources," GAO warned.

HHS received six recommendations, the most of any agency reviewed, after investigators found that it lacked a documented enterprise-wide zero trust implementation plan covering all its information systems.

Although individual divisions were pursuing cybersecurity improvements, GAO warned that the absence of a unified strategy could prevent department leadership from maintaining a coherent view of its security modernization efforts.
HHS agreed with the recommendations and said it planned to develop an actionable department-wide strategy by the second quarter of fiscal year 2027.
CHINESE HACKERS TARGET NASA AND KEY US AGENCIES, DOJ ALLEGES
The Department of Commerce received four recommendations after investigators identified shortcomings in its cybersecurity planning documentation .

Commerce officials told GAO that staffing losses had significantly constrained the department's zero trust working group, limiting its ability to coordinate improvements and maintain comprehensive documentation.

At DHS, investigators found that the department had not fully documented cybersecurity maturity levels across all its high-value assets and high-impact systems. Officials attributed the incomplete assessments partly to lengthy government shutdowns during the preceding fiscal year.
DHS INVESTIGATES MASSIVE DATA BREACH EXPOSING 40,000 EMPLOYEES, INCLUDING ICE AND BORDER PATROL AGENTS

DOJ similarly cited resource constraints for incomplete assessments of critical systems, while State and Treasury were among the agencies that had only partially documented cybersecurity maturity levels.
GAO warned that incomplete assessments could leave agency leadership without the visibility necessary to determine where additional cybersecurity resources are needed.

Investigators also found that 11 agencies had only partially documented procedures for identifying actors within their IT environments, including certain non-person entities such as software applications and service accounts.
The watchdog warned that incomplete identification procedures could hinder efforts to ensure only authorized users and systems access government resources.
TRUMP’S NATIONAL CYBER DIRECTOR SEAN CAIRNCROSS FIRED AMID WIDESPREAD TECH OUTAGES

The findings come years after the Biden administration directed federal agencies to adopt zero trust cybersecurity principles through a 2021 executive order, followed by additional guidance in 2022 and 2024. Despite those directives, GAO found that 17 of 22 agencies still had not fully addressed selected cybersecurity planning requirements and guidance as of August 2026.

Thirteen agencies agreed with GAO's 40 recommendations, while four neither agreed nor disagreed. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission, one of the four, provided documentation demonstrating that it had already addressed both recommendations, which GAO verified.
Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and all 17 agencies identified in the report for comment.
"Absent a full implementation of ZTA requirements and guidance, agencies will lack an appropriate roadmap to fully incorporate and maintain an effective zero trust architecture," GAO concluded.

articles.headline: Attention Pixel 9 and 10 owners: is it actually worth upgrading to the Pixel 11?
keyFacts: The Google Pixel 11 launched in August 2026 for $899, offering minor hardware improvements over the Pixel 10.
Reviewers suggest Pixel 10 owners skip the upgrade, while Pixel 9 owners may benefit from the new telephoto lens and improved battery life.
Google provides seven years of software updates for all three models, meaning older devices remain supported for several more years.
body: Attention Pixel 9 and 10 owners: is it actually worth upgrading to the Pixel 11?
Pixel 10 owners can skip this one. Pixel 9 owners have a real decision to make.

Google's new Pixel 11 went on sale in August 2026, but new doesn't always mean better. It uses the same 6.3-inch display and 5x telephoto camera as the previous year's model; has the same 12GB of RAM; and its battery is just 15mAh bigger. You'll enjoy double the storage space, but it also costs $899, which is $100 more than the launch price of the Pixel 10.

If the question is whether it's worth upgrading from the 10 to the 11, the answer is no. Keep the phone you've got. If you're a Pixel 9 owner, the advantages are more pronounced. Jumping two generations gets you a telephoto lens, better battery life and an additional two years of software updates, making the upgrade a worthy consideration.
What's new compared to the Pixel 10

With the Pixel 11, you get a Tensor G6 chip, which replaces last year's Tensor G5. Google claims the G6 gives users 25 percent improvements in web browsing speed, alongside 15 percent improvements in app launches. The 48MP main camera gets a larger sensor that's reportedly 56 percent more sensitive to light, and Super Zoom reaches 30x instead of 20x. Wireless charging has increased from 15W to 25W, and the phone now comes with 256GB rather than 128GB.

While 30x zoom sounds impressive, our hands-on testing found that these zoom shots looked fine on the phone's screen but lost a lot of detail once we opened them on a laptop. The phone itself was quick and fluid, though admittedly nothing we threw at it pushed it very hard.

On its comparison page with the Pixel 10, Google lists two camera features as exclusive to the Pixel 11: Magic Capture and Camera Looks. Magic Capture records a short clip and pulls out the best frames as stills, while Camera Looks lets you set and tweak a default filter. However, Android Central's Harish Jonnalagadda argues that most of this year's software additions will reach older Pixels through Google's regular updates anyway. Once you take those away (or, rather, add them to the Pixel 10), you may be essentially paying for a faster chip, double the base memory and quicker wireless charging. That's hard to justify at $899, especially if you bought the Pixel 10 in 2025.
It's a different story for Pixel 9 owners

The Pixel 9 has two rear cameras, a 50MP main and a 48MP ultrawide, and tops out at 8x Super Res Zoom. To that, the Pixel 11 adds a 10.8MP telephoto camera with a 5x optical zoom and optical image stabilization. That's more optical reach than the $799 iPhone 17, which has no telephoto at all, or the $899 Galaxy S26, whose 10MP telephoto stops at 3x. When we reviewed the Pixel 11, that telephoto was its main advantage over phones at the same price. It's not a Pro camera, though. The Pixel 11 Pro's telephoto uses a 48MP, 1/1.95-inch sensor, while the base model makes do with a 1/3.2-inch sensor.

In terms of its battery, the Pixel 9 has a 4,700mAh that Google rates for more than 24 hours, while the Pixel 11's 4,985mAh cell is rated for more than 30 hours. In our testing, the Pixel 11 lasted from 8AM on a Saturday to 7PM on Sunday on a single charge. You'll also get Pixelsnap magnets built in with the 11, so magnetic Qi2 chargers and mounts attach without a case, which can't be done with the Pixel 9. The 11's screen is also brighter, peaking at 3,000 nits against the Pixel 9's 2,700.
Google Pixel software support

Google promises seven years of OS and security updates from the date each Pixel first went on sale in the United States. That puts the end of software updates for the Pixel 9 at August 2031, the Pixel 10 at August 2032 and the Pixel 11 at August 2033, so none of these models are anywhere near being left behind yet. If you're struggling with your Pixel 9's battery life, something which has admittedly led me to prematurely upgrade my phone in the past, a genuine replacement will set you back about $50 at iFixit. Google can also provide price quotes for its mail-in repair service through an online estimator.

In our opinion, Pixel 10 owners should definitely consider hanging on until at least the Pixel 12 because, as we said earlier, you're not getting that much more for your money. The telephoto lens is the real draw for Pixel 9 owners who could benefit from having better zoom — a feature that no software update can add. But if your Pixel 9 still gets you through the day and you rarely venture beyond 2x zoom, there's no pressing reason to fork out $899 right now.

articles.headline: Binding Of Isaac Update Review-Bombed Over AI-Generated Music In GTA 6 Mode: ‘Woke Up To A Sh*t Show, Obviously I Had No Idea’
keyFacts: The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+ update was review-bombed after players discovered AI-generated music in a new GTA-inspired game mode.
Game creator Edmund McMillen stated he was unaware of the AI music and is working to remove it from the game.
Publisher Nicalis has not yet addressed the inclusion of the AI assets or the lack of required disclosure on the Steam store page.
body: The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+ was a free update to the beloved roguelike that arrived on PC in 2024, but launched on console earlier this week in a head-to-head matchup against Grand Theft Auto 6. The marketing stunt may have been a success, but AI-generated music tracks discovered in a special new Vice City mode have turned the launch into a nightmare.

While Repentance+ came to PS5, Xbox Series X/S, and Switch 2 this week, the Steam version of the game also got a free update. “Be sure to get in and play today’s Daily Run for a very special crime-packed surprise. Enter the Basement, and go out in a glorious blaze of bullets and vehicular homicide!” read the patch notes on on Valve’s storefront. Players could enter the seed “V1CE BSMT” into the roguelike before starting their run to launch a GTA-inspired version with special weapons and music.

Earlier today, however, Reddit user ShweetsStuff posted a comprehensive breakdown of the new music tracks alleging they were made with Suno, an AI-based music generation tool. “The new update includes 14 music files for the run; seven full songs, plus some derivatives (intros/outros),” the wrote. The post continued:

Some include Suno metadata with them. You can find this information yourself by just checking the file comment metadata (something common like VLC has tools for this, but here’s ffprobe output of drivingsong1.ogg, for example):
comment : made with suno; created=2026-10-30T17:53:41Z; id=cd5a5b55-bead-4cb9-949d-09ed1f917dce
Other files have this comment scrubbed; they were edited/exported later, but nonetheless there’s the proof.
Please report issues and bugs to the email attached. https://t.co/KHKSqKGsUe
— ð Edmund McMillen ð (@edmundmcmillen) November 21, 2026

“They’ve had how long now to prepare the GTA 6 release Easter egg daily run literally nobody asked for and still ai slopped it? Are you fucking kidding me,” one fan wrote on the Binding of Isaac subreddit. “No shit, itâs 2026. The entire industry is like this. Cutting corners constantly because they know they can get away with it,” wrote another.

Many have blamed Nicalis, the publisher and co-developer of the Repentance+ expansion, in particular. Complaints about ongoing bugs, latency, and quality control issues have seemingly been building for some time. The latest mishap results in a review-bomb of the expansion’s Steam page, which currently sits at an abysmal user rating of just 9 percent positive. “AI generated music in GTA mode; Edmund please take back control of the game,” reads one of the latest Steam reviews. “Not to mention there’s like single digit bug fixes in a year+ long awaited update with no other changes.”

The AI music was news to Edmund McMillen, the game’s creator. “Woke up to a shit show, obviously I had no idea it featured generated music in the daily run, looking into how that happened and getting it removed, stay tuned,” he posted earlier today on X. An emergency update has since gone out to remove the AI-generated music as well as address some other versions with the latest version of the expansion, but Nicalis has yet to take responsibility for the use of AI or explained how it made it into the game.

Steam requires store page disclosures for any content that uses assets generated with the help of AI, which The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+Â did not have, despite the big publicity push around the latest update and it landing on the same day as Rockstar’s open-world blockbuster. “That was [Nicalis’] idea,” McMillen recently told Eurogamer. “‘Wouldn’t it be funny if…?’ I was like, whatever, that’s funny…We’re done, so we’ve got to release this month…It’s a fun experiment.”

“Obviously he had to come off. We are worried, but we don’t know. Tomorrow [Sunday], he will have an MRI.”
The injury has come three days before Arsenal return to Champions League action with a home clash against Borussia Dortmund.
As it stands, Arrizabalaga looks set to start between the sticks on Tuesday night.
He has featured in the competition on just one occasion for Arsenal since signing from rivals Chelsea in 2025.
That appearance came in their last league phase match at home to Kazakhstan-based FC Kairat last season, which ended in a 3-2 win for Arsenal.

articles.headline: Alt Video is a digital, faux Blockbuster video store that you can fill with movies from your Letterboxd watchlist and Plex server
keyFacts: Alt Video is a digital simulation game that allows users to populate a virtual video store with movies from Letterboxd or Plex servers.
The game features a cinema room for watching films with friends and supports VR, manual item additions, and various themed environments.
Alt Video will launch in early access on Steam on November 24th with plans to add store management features in the future.
body: Since the beginning of the year, I have watched almost 150 films. I know this, because over the past few years, I've become one of those people… a Letterboxd user. Gasp! I know, I know, but I don't think I'm too insufferable about it. I'll only do a joke review in the hopes of like farming if I think it's genuinely funny! But many of these films were watched digitally, meaning I don't have a bunch of DVDs to admire on a shelf. So what am I to do? Well, I could check out Alt Video, a not quite job simulator where you can use your Letterboxd account or media server to fill up a digital, faux Blockbuster.

This is, obviously, not so dissimilar to Boxroom, a game where you can design your own bedroom that lets you use your Steam profile to fill it with games you actually own. With Alt Video, you do things slightly differently just because of the focus on a different format. So, say you have a Letterboxd account. After exporting some data from your account, you can bring that into Alt Video, and this fake video store will then get filled up with shelves of DVD cases of all the films you've watched.

Alternatively, and perhaps more enticingly, if you run something like a Plex or Jellyfin server, you can hook that up to the game too, where again all of the films you own digitally show up in store. What's more interesting here is that there's a cinema room in the store that lets you watch films on your Plex server, and it's possible to invite your Steam friends to watch along with you. There's even a few other rooms, like a '90s bedroom or family room for more of a CRT kinda vibe. It's cute! If you like you can even manually add any DVDs or Blu-rays you own to appear on all the shelves too.

There's a lot of other nice touches too. In the case of your Letterboxd data, your ratings even show up on the back of the boxes. It's not just relegated to films either, you can put in shows or even your games. The whole thing can be played in VR if you really want that immersive feel. There's a store clerk who can give you some recommendations if you're not sure what to watch. And there's even a day and night system, weather, and seasonal shopfront facelifts.

Alt Video is currently slated for release next week on November 24th, and it'll be doing so in early access. Worth noting that for now the focus is on the browsing, but features involving serving customers and running the store are on the way. You can wishlist it on Steam right here.

articles.headline: Review: Godzilla Minus Zero joins the list of truly stellar sequels
keyFacts: Director Takashi Yamazaki has released Godzilla Minus Zero, a sequel to his 2023 film Godzilla Minus One.
The new film features human themes and kaiju battles, following the success of the original which earned $116 million and an Oscar.
The sequel continues the story of pilot Kōichi Shikishima and addresses the regeneration of Godzilla's remains teased at the end of the first movie.
body: It’s a rare thing for a film sequel to match or even surpass its predecessor; The Godfather Part II and Terminator 2: Judgement Day are the best known examples on a pretty short list. Go ahead and add Godzilla Minus Zero to that list. Director Takashi Yamazaki’s sequel to his critically acclaimed Godzilla Minus One (2023) is everything one could want in a Godzilla movie: human pathos, great special effects, and, ultimately, two giant kaiju duking it out over who gets to destroy Japan (and eventually the world) the most.
(Spoilers for the first film below. Spoilers for Minus Zero but no major reveals until after the gallery. We’ll give you a heads-up when we get there.)

As I wrote previously, Yamazaki wanted to return to Godzilla’s filmic roots with Minus One, setting the events in postwar Japan and tapping into the monster’s symbolic representation of the Japanese perspective on the 1940s nuclear holocaust—while also incorporating all-too-human themes of guilt and redemption. That first film focused on kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who struggled with survivor’s guilt after he failed to take action when Godzilla attacked the Japanese base on Odo Island in 1945.

Knocked unconscious, Kōichi survived and awoke to find his parents and many others were killed in the World War II bombing of Tokyo. Kōichi rebuilt a life with a woman named Noriko (Minami Hamabe) and the orphaned baby she rescued, Akiko (Sae Nagatani). But then Godzilla re-emerged, and Kōichi resolved to die fighting the monster to atone for Odo Island. Kōichi saved the day and lived to tell the tale. He reunited with Noriko, who had a strange black bruise on her neck. And we saw a chunk of Godzilla’s remains start to regenerate, leaving things open for a sequel.

Godzilla Minus One was a massive hit, both in Japan—where it remains one of the highest grossing Japanese films ever—and worldwide, racking up $116 million globally and winning an Oscar for best visual effects. Yamazaki said in interviews at the time that there had as yet been no talk of a sequel—while also hinting at future directions a sequel might explore. He later admitted it was way of planting a seed for what would become Godzilla Minus Zero.

articles.headline: What did Xi Jinping get from the bear hug with Trump at the Shenzhen summit?
keyFacts: U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin met at a summit in Shenzhen.
Analyst Robert Daly said Xi Jinping gained performative prestige from hosting the summit, while Putin sought equal standing with two superpowers.
Daly stated that Trump prompted Xi Jinping to agree to future talks on reducing nuclear risks.
body: What did Xi Jinping get from the bear hug with Trump at the Shenzhen summit?
NPR's Rob Schmitz speaks with Robert Daly, director of the program on US China relations at University of Maryland's School of Public Policy, about President Trump's trip to China this week.
ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:

When the president goes on a big diplomatic trip, it's not always clear what's happening in all those meetings they go to. That was true during President Trump's trip to China this week, but there were intriguing public moments.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
UNIDENTIFIED CHILDREN: (Chanting in non-English language).
SCHMITZ: A group of children chanted, warm welcome, over and over, as Xi Jinping met Trump on the tarmac. Now add a third leader to the mix.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: Who is he? He's my friend.

SCHMITZ: That was Vladimir Putin, who's also a friend of Xi Jinping's, though the two may preside over an uneasy alliance. The stakes were high. Trump is looking for a breakthrough on nuclear weapons control. The U.S. and China are in a faceoff over AI, and a deal to end the bloodshed in Ukraine has been elusive.

Now that the summit's over, we're joined by someone who can help make sense of what happened. Robert Daly was a U.S. foreign service officer in China and now directs the program on U.S.-China relations at the University of Maryland School of Public Policy. And he's here with me in the studio. Welcome.
ROBERT DALY: Good to be here. Thank you.
SCHMITZ: So what did Xi Jinping want out of this meeting?

DALY: Xi Jinping - as always, his first goal is performative. It is to have the Chinese people see him as a world leader, beneficent, competent, hosting others who are coming somewhat cap in hand, at least in a very friendly way, to China. There's a very ancient saying in Chinese, (speaking Chinese), which means the 10,000 kingdoms all come to the center here. And Xi has been hosting an awful lot of leaders recently.
SCHMITZ: How'd he do?

DALY: He did very well from the Chinese point of view. I think that the hug of Donald Trump - we tend to see that from an American point of view as being friendly. Now, whether that's performative, friendship or truly felt is only for them to say. But for the Chinese, that's an unusually warm and humanizing move for Xi. Even the Chinese people will complain that their leaders are often too stayed, too in control. And this warmth, I think, also makes him look good, as does all the formal ceremony.
SCHMITZ: We also had Vladimir Putin there, the president of Russia. What was his goal at this meeting?

DALY: Well, this appears to have been his idea. His goal as the head of what is now, at least in many spheres - not in China, but in the West - a rogue nation that has invaded Ukraine - he gets a place of honor with what are unquestionably the world's only two superpowers, but as if perhaps he's in their league, which, other than his possession of nuclear weapons, he really isn't.
SCHMITZ: Was he treated like he was in their league during this meeting?
DALY: Well, this has been controversial within Russia itself. Some Russians on the internet have felt that he was dissed. He didn't get a meeting at the airport the way that Trump did. He didn't...
SCHMITZ: Right.
DALY: ...Get bear hugged this time in public, although he has met with Xi Jinping about 50 times now. So he's been warmly greeted overall, but he didn't get quite the same status.
SCHMITZ: And it's important to point out here that, especially in Russia and in China, people often look for these symbolic gestures because there's not much to go on.
China and Russia have called their partnership unbreakable in the past. Was that alliance meaningful at this summit?

DALY: Yes, and it has been meaningful really ever since the invasion of Ukraine. Tony Binken has said that China is the essential enabler for that invasion, both because it buys a lot of oil and gas, but also because it sells many, many dual-use parts to Russia, which enables it to improve its drones, but it also keeps it afloat economically.
SCHMITZ: I mentioned the small but significant detail that Xi met Trump on the runway. Did you spot any other moments at this summit that also caught your attention?

DALY: After the meeting on the runway, what I was listening for was whether Xi Jinping would describe Trump as a great friend or a great and wise leader - all the things that Trump says about Xi, which are never reciprocated. Xi sort of pockets the compliment. He smiles...
SCHMITZ: (Laughter).

DALY: ...In an oracular way, and on we go. And so I was wondering, would that hug be followed up by protestations of friendship? And I didn't really hear that. And if you look at the Chinese government readout of the three-way meeting, it's just blandishments about the need for peace and friendship.
SCHMITZ: That's interesting. So what you noticed is something that actually didn't happen?
DALY: He doesn't return the compliments.
SCHMITZ: What does that mean for the overall U.S.-China relationship in the eyes of someone like Xi Jinping, who's leading this country forward?
DALY: Well, Xi, as I see it - he's not inclined to discuss his emotions or his feelings about even fellow Chinese ever.
SCHMITZ: Right.
DALY: There's a sense that as a leader of 1.4 billion, he should sort of be above personality...
SCHMITZ: OK.

DALY: ...And not show any of that. So it's part and parcel of that. But also if you compliment me and I don't return the compliment, there's a sense in which I win, right? At least in Chinese - in terms of Chinese political culture, that's true.

SCHMITZ: I sort of feel like this - were three leaders that were just saying, hey, how are you doing? You know, you look great. We're all great partners. And there wasn't really much something substantive coming out of this.

DALY: President Trump did get them to speak publicly about nuclear weapons, and this gives a thin but an important foundation perhaps for later talks. China is nowhere near ready to talk about reducing its nuclear weapons. They continue to build and will until they get parity in about 10 years. But Xi Jinping did agree to talk about reducing nuclear risks. That's left vague, and they're talking about nonproliferation, but it opens the door. It opens the door a crack, and I think that's a good thing.
SCHMITZ: Anything that maybe worried you about this summit?

DALY: Well, the question is, you know, whether President Trump is now setting a precedent for the way that other American leaders will behave vis-a-vis China. When you get these descriptions of friendship - Xi Jinping is a great leader, China is a great country - if the next guy doesn't repeat those phrases, then that will seem like a falling off.

We seem to be going more and more for performance. In fact, all American presidents who have visited China have always been pleasant and respectful. Trump didn't invent this. But they've also described American interests, American values, America's dissatisfaction with China.

And that's been OK. The Chinese don't expect the Americans to be exactly like them. But now Trump, I worry, is setting a precedent that makes it difficult to talk about the real problems we all face, and he doesn't seem to have done that at this meeting.
SCHMITZ: That is Robert Daly. He's the director of the China and United States Program at University of Maryland School of Public Policy. Thanks so much for coming in.
DALY: Thank you.

articles.headline: Amazon is complaining about NYC Council on shipping labels, too
keyFacts: Amazon is placing labels on shipping packages claiming that New York City Council legislation could increase customer order costs by up to five dollars.
The proposed Delivery Protection Act would require last-mile delivery firms to be licensed by the city and directly employ their workers.
Amazon warned the bill could cause slower, more expensive deliveries, while city officials and labor unions accused the company of using intimidation tactics.
body: Amazon is leaving no venue unexplored in its fight against the New York City Council and the Delivery Protection Act. The company is now putting labels on shipments claiming that the Council could add up to $5 to any Amazon order. The Delivery Protection Act would effectively ban the sort of third-party arrangements Amazon currently uses to deliver many packages, including small companies and independent contractors. Last-mile delivery firms operating warehouses would need to be licensed by the city and directly employ their workers.
Amazon is complaining about NYC Council on shipping labels, too
Amazon is taking its accusations that the Council is driving up prices offline and onto your packages.

Earlier this week, Amazon started showing notifications in its mobile app and on its website reading “Attention NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.” Now the company is including an almost identical message on shipping labels.

Amazon claims that the bill, if passed, “would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City,” and has threatened to move its warehouses outside of the city. However, labor unions, Council Speaker Julie Menin, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani have countered that the company is attempting to “threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council” and is acting out of “greed,” pointing to Amazon’s market cap of nearly $3 trillion.

articles.headline: Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance
keyFacts: Signal is restricting screenshot capabilities on Android and iOS to prevent operating system AI from scanning screen data.
Signal President Meredith Whittaker called screen-scanning AI agents an existential threat to the app's ability to guarantee privacy.
Users can disable the screenshot restriction, but Whittaker noted this breaks Signal's privacy guarantees and is an incomplete solution.
body: Signal announced Friday that it’s limiting users’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI.

Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”

“Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she said. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”
Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default. Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS.

That said, users can disable this setting if they wish, which Whittaker said would “break our privacy guarantees.” She also admitted this is an “incomplete” solution, as it doesn’t “address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data.”

articles.headline: California prosecutor rips Newsom’s death row decision, citing technicality for SoCal prisoners
keyFacts: Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer asked the California Supreme Court to review Governor Gavin Newsom's commutations of 18 death row inmates.
Spitzer argued that Newsom granted mass clemency based on personal opposition to capital punishment rather than reviewing cases individually.
The California Supreme Court is preparing to review commutations involving inmates with multiple felony convictions, the article reported.
body: A prominent California district attorney is taking a swing at Gov. Gavin Newsom’s sweeping death row commutations — targeting 18 convicted killers from Orange County, including a notorious serial murderer and a child killer.
Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer filed a new request with the California Supreme Court Friday, urging justices to review Newsom’s decision to spare the 18 inmates from execution.

The latest challenge focuses on prisoners who had no prior felony convictions before the murders that landed them on death row. Unlike inmates with multiple felony convictions, their commutations do not automatically require approval from the state’s high court.
Advertisement
Of the 584 condemned inmates statewide who received Newsom’s clemency, 202 are set to have their sentences commuted without additional court approval, according to Spitzer’s office.
Spitzer argued in his filing that Newsom’s mass commutations were driven by his personal opposition to capital punishment rather than a case-by-case review of the law.
The governor effectively acted because he “disagrees with the law,” Spitzer argued, noting that California voters have twice rejected ballot measures to abolish the death penalty.
Advertisement

“Our criminal justice system does not bend with the political winds, and one man – even if he is the governor – does not get to put his thumb on the scales of justice simply because he does not like the law,” Spitzer said in a statement.
“I refuse to allow one man to dismantle our criminal justice system brick by brick and sentence by sentence until there is not a shred of accountability left.”
Spitzer also accused Newsom of failing to “faithfully execute” the law by granting sweeping clemency instead of evaluating the inmates’ cases individually.
Advertisement

The 18 prisoners who were sentenced to death in the county without having prior felonies are Maria del Rosio Alfaro, Ika Amulu, Alejandro Avila, Eric Wayne Bennett, Richard Delmer Boyer, Shaun Kareem Burney, Edward Charles III, Richard Lucio DeHoyos, John Joseph Famalaro, Randy Steven Kraft, Waymon Livingston, Victor Mirando Miranda-Guerrero, Christian Antonio Monterroso, Iftekhar Murtaza, Tanya Jaime Nelson, Ignacio Arriola Tafoya, Eduardo David Vargas and Daniel Patrick Wozniak.
For example, Bennett was sentenced to death in 1997 for the 1994 rape and murder of 50-year-old Marie Evans Powell.
Advertisement

Bennett— who had installed flooring or carpet at Powell’s Laguna Hills townhouse two weeks earlier— burglarized her home, raped her and fatally bludgeoned her. He was also convicted of raping and robbing another woman at knifepoint in Costa Mesa.

Kraft is a notorious serial killer who committed the rape, torture and murder of a minimum of sixteen young men across Southern California between 1972 and 1983. Investigators have also linked him or suspected him in dozens of additional killings, with estimates ranging up to 67 total victims across three states.

Avila is a convicted murderer who kidnapped, sexually assaulted, and killed 5-year-old Samantha Runnion in Stanton, California, in 2002. Avila abducted the child while she was playing outside her home. Her body was found the following day about 50 miles away in Riverside County.
Advertisement
But the latest legal challenge could face questions over whether the state’s constitution gives Newsom clear authority to commute the sentences of inmates with no prior felony convictions.

Attorney Scott Sanders, who represents Wozniak, questioned the purpose of Spitzer’s filing, telling City News Service: “I’m not exactly sure what the goal is in filing the brief. The law appears to be completely settled on this issue in terms of a governor’s right to commute.”
Newsom has defended his sweeping decision as a matter of conscience, arguing that he was morally compelled to spare the condemned inmates.
“But the constitution also gave every governor clemency authority, and that power exists for moments when law as applied cannot be squared with justice. For me, this is that moment,” Newsom wrote.
Victim advocacy groups have separately taken their objections to the state Supreme Court as it prepares to review commutations involving inmates with multiple felony convictions.

Crime Victims United on Friday asked Associate Justice Kelli Evans to recuse herself from that process, because she formerly worked for Newsom and reportedly helped create his 2019 executive order placing a moratorium on executions, which is still in place.
The justice swiftly denied that request, prompting outcry from advocates for an explanation. The Post reached out to the state supreme court for comment.

articles.headline: Trump orders contractors to check with White House over any congressional inquiries
keyFacts: Donald Trump issued an executive order requiring federal contractors to consult with the administration regarding inquiries received from Congress, according to the order.
The White House stated that the order protects executive privileges from congressional overreach ahead of expected investigations by Democrats in January.
Companies that fail to comply could have their federal contracts terminated and future government work suspended, the White House warned.
body: Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to an executive order issued late Friday.

The companies must also coordinate with the White House and US agencies on “appropriate responses” to any such requests, the order says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns, their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended.

The order signed late Friday is the administration’s latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January. Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets , noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Trump’s family, particularly at the Pentagon.

It comes as White House officials have already begun taking steps to exert more control over how agencies and officials respond to congressional requests, anticipating there will be a flood of investigations once Democrats take power in January.

On Monday, Will Scharf, the White House counsel, told US agencies that they must seek approval from his office and the White House’s office of legislative affairs before agreeing to appear before Congress. Scharf also suggested in a recent letter to the US representative Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, that some congressional investigations may amount to “blatant criminality”.

Garcia earlier this week sent letters directing members of Trump’s family and top administration officials to preserve documents. Scharf sought to dismiss the requests, noting in a letter to Democratic lawmakers that they are not yet in the majority and cannot compel compliance.

In a fact sheet, the White House framed the new requirements as “protecting executive privileges from congressional overreach”, arguing that some congressional leaders have tried to intrude on executive branch privileges by “harassing private companies that contract with the federal government”.

Presidents of both parties have long used executive privilege to resist congressional inquiries, but the claims can set up messy, protracted legal fights as parties dispute whether it applies. Executive privilege allows the president to keep information from the courts, Congress and the public to protect the confidentiality of White House deliberations, but the protection is far from absolute.
Friday’s executive order applies to all contractors and subcontractors, a universe of tens of thousands of businesses.

articles.headline: Unannounced Nioh 3 Complete Edition has been rated in Korea
keyFacts: South Korea's game rating board has rated an unannounced Nioh 3 Complete Edition, according to a listing spotted by Insider Gaming.
The GRAC listing describes the game as a compilation of additional content for the dark Sengoku action RPG and assigns it a 19+ rating for violence.
Koei Tecmo has not yet officially announced the Complete Edition, and Eurogamer has contacted the publisher for comment.
body: A rating for the unannounced Nioh 3 Complete Edition has popped up on Korea's Game Rating and Administration Committee (GRAC).

As Insider Gaming spotted, the board gave Nioh 3 Complete Edition a 19+ rating on 17th November after it was submitted on 2nd November, even though Koei Tecmo hasn't announced a Complete Edition for the game yet.

The listing, translated by machine, describes it as "a compilation of additional content from the dark Sengoku action RPG Nioh 3", and gives the rating for "excessive expression of violence", noting that "red blood and body amputation frequently occur during combat".
The listing also notes an overseas rating, which Insider Gaming says is a 17+ rating from Japan's CERO.
Unlike some rating boards, GRAC publishes its ratings as soon as they're decided, which is why game listings often surface there before they're officially announced.

If Koei Tecmo follows the same pattern as Nioh 2, there may not be long to wait. GRAC's records show Nioh 2 was rated in January 2020, and its Complete Edition followed in November that year. Nioh 3 was rated on 14th November 2025, almost exactly a year ago.

Complete Editions typically includes the base game and all of its DLC. It could even launch alongside Nioh 3's second DLC, Bloody Insurrection, which is due in February 2027. Eurogamer has contacted Koei Tecmo for comment and we'll let you know if/when they come back to us.

Back in April, an update introduced "multiple high-difficulty Battle Scrolls" (side missions), accessible from shrines, the addition of a Stone of Penance item "which increases accessory +Values and rarities in exchange for higher difficulties", and new skills given as rewards for completing the aforementioned high-level Battle Scroll missions.

Eurogamer's review of Nioh 3 called the threequel a new high for the 'masocore' series and "the crucible in which all of Team Ninja's experience has been siphoned into." It's sold over one million copies (and counting) since its 6th February launch.

articles.headline: Bill Maher Casts Doubt On Trump Admins Explanation For FAA Outage
keyFacts: Talk show host Bill Maher questioned the Trump administration's stated reason for a recent nationwide FAA flight ground stop.
Maher suggested on his show that the government might not publicly disclose a truly alarming cause for the aviation outage.
Maher also acknowledged that the administration's explanation involving a systems changeover remains a plausible possibility.
body: “Real Time” host Bill Maher cast doubt on the Trump administration’s stated reason for last week’s FAA outage that prompted a nationwide ground stop on flights in the U.S.

Speaking with MS NOW host Jacob Soboroff and Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido (D-Texas), Maher theorized that if the FAA ground stop was something that would alarm the general public, the government wouldn’t say so publicly.
“They wouldn’t really tell us if it was, right? Can we agree that if you think it’s something other than what they’re telling us, it may be a conspiracy theory, but it’s not a crazy one,” Maher said.
Soboroff, who reported from Los Angeles International Airport during the ground stop, described the general feeling of uncertainty as the situation unfolded.

“I stood at the airport, and I reported live last Friday as everybody was in the dark about all of this,” Soboroff said. “And the one thing you want from your elected leaders, whether it’s in Washington or on a local level, is for them to give you information that can enlighten you and help you understand the world around us.”
The MS NOW host noted that the administration refused to rule anything out, including a potential cyberattack, in the early hours of the crisis.
Maher said that while it’s not crazy to question the administration’s explanation, the truth could also be very well what they’re telling the public.

“They’re saying it’s a changeover in systems. This is also very plausible, is it not?” the comedian asked. “Let’s not get hysterical about this. This happens at my house all the time. Do you not sometimes have your TV just tell you, ‘Uh, I’m taking a personal day’?”
Soboroff then added a sobering thought to the conversation.

“If this is what happens when nothing nefarious is going down, and this is the reaction of the government and of the people, imagine what happens when there is a hostile actor that comes into this country and does something that puts us in a position that’s far, far worse,” Soboroff said.

articles.headline: AWS got hit by an outage too. Here's why you didn't hear about it
keyFacts: On November 15, AWS confirmed an incident in its us-east-1 region that disrupted 11 services between 3:05 AM and 6:53 AM PST.
The disruption went largely unnoticed because it affected engineers signing into AWS accounts rather than consumer apps on pre-dawn Sunday.
Larger simultaneous outages at Microsoft and nationwide air traffic control also drew public attention away from the AWS incident.
body: My editor asked me this week "why is everything except AWS breaking?"

It's a great question! They haven't been in the headlines! In fact, as they are wont to do, AWS spokesperson Patrick Neighorn g ot salty to a reporter about how unreliable Downdetector is when it started showing them as impacted.

If you'll permit me a small digression, this stems from a misunderstanding of what Downdetector is for. Historically the AWS status site was so hilariously slow to reflect the lived customer experience that some jackass (me) built a rewriter that sits at stop.lying.cloud to make it a smidgen more realistic. As a result, the question people are really trying to answer when they visit Downdetector is "my app just broke; is it my crappy code or is there a global event going on?" There are mitigations for both, but they look nothing alike.

AWS view crowdsourced reports of the form "the internet is broken, must be AWS" as a stain upon their honor. In fact, it's a badge of their own success, as "the internet" and "AWS" have become inextricably linked in people's minds.
But back to my editor's question, "why didn't AWS go down?"
Easy: it did.
Everything breaks, all the time, including the narrative

AWS now has 34 generally available commercial regions, of which two are currently smoking craters due to the Iran conflict. Each of these has hundreds of services that AWS offers to customers, of which a dozen or so are high quality, if I'm being characteristically uncharitable. They experience degradation in various ways, and they go largely unnoticed.
But on November 15, AWS confirmed an incident that disrupted 11 of those ~12 good services in their oldest and most important region, us-east-1.

At 3:05 AM PST, they stated that they started seeing sign-up errors, authentication issues, and connectivity issues. Five minutes later engineers were engaged. Not to be outdone, their status page swung into action after a leisurely coffee, and posted its first indication of an incident 93 minutes later. (See previous comments on stop.lying.cloud ). The all-clear showed up at 6:53 AM.

Every site has downtime. Sometimes it blows up publicly, other times nobody seems to notice. Heck, AWS said in September that it had experienced permanent data loss in its two smoking craters, but after that news cycle passed I haven't heard a thing about it. I do think it's patently unreasonable to blame them for this specific problem; "acts of war" are kinda hard to predict from the corporate planning meeting.
A few things combined to help AWS out on November 15. First, it was pre-dawn Pacific time on Sunday. Most of us slept through it; my kids aren't even up that early.
Further, the services that were most impacted (IAM Identity Center) were for engineers signing in to AWS accounts, not consumers staring at an app that stopped working.

Plus, the competition sucked all the oxygen out of the room: a day-plus Microsoft 365 364 outage and a four-hour nationwide air traffic ground stop had done a great job of level-setting what kind of outage was going to get attention, and "us-east-1 being weird but the apps still work" doesn't cut it.

Downdetector – which is owned by Accenture , so it's not like AWS doesn't have a throat to choke if they want to stop picking on reporters – measures consumer screaming. Originally, it was largely Twitter semantic analytics. This isn't a bad thing! As I said, I want to know if the internet is breaking. We can sort out exactly what part later.
The November 15 outage didn't produce that kind of screaming. Ironically, the tool that AWS is complaining about in the newspaper is the reason they skated by without notice on this outage.
Counterintuitively, Downdetector reports that outages have decreased since about 2022. Instead, what we're seeing is large-scale centralization.

Our companies don't run email systems internally anymore; we outsource to large technology companies who are almost universally better at fixing and resolving large-scale issues than we will be internally. And it feels unkind to dunk on those hard-working folks for their outages; would we want them to dunk on us for ours?
("Wait, don't you own stop.lying.cloud ?" "Do as I say, not as I do.")

But whether anyone notices depends upon what layer broke, and when. If my company's email system broke on Monday, and your company's email system broke on Tuesday, the story would stop at "computers suck." But when everyone's email system goes down at once, the world takes notice.

Microsoft had to tell the whole world about a bug it mostly sat on since July. AWS hasn't had to tell anyone anything. My editor runs a tech publication that covers this stuff for a living and didn't know. You can't buy PR like this, and AWS didn't have to.
If I were AWS, I'd stop complaining about Downdetector and send it a fruit basket. ®

articles.headline: Is Raphael Warnock running for president?
keyFacts: Sen. Raphael Warnock stated he is keeping options open regarding a potential 2028 Democratic presidential bid.
Warnock explained that Democrats can win in the South by visiting rural communities and building multiracial coalitions around shared concerns.
Warnock emphasized that resolving tough international issues like the Israeli-Palestinian conflict requires strong American presidential leadership.
body: Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-GA) has kept the door open on a presidential bid. | Finn Gomez/Getty Images

The 2026 midterm elections were less than three weeks ago — and the new Democratic congressional majorities chosen by voters are still more than a month from taking office — but if the 2028 Democratic presidential primary isn’t fully underway, then at the very least, potential candidates are already starting to jockey for position.

Some of that maneuvering was on display earlier this month at the fittingly named “What’s Next” political conference in Denver. The conference drew Democratic operatives, strategists, and presidential hopefuls from around the country — and Vox’s America, Actually podcast, where host Astead Herndon asked attendees for their thoughts about Democratic Party’s future.

Herndon also sat down with one possible 2028 candidate: Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-GA). His background is especially relevant after the midterms: He’s the senior pastor at the historic Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta at a time when more Democratic candidates are embracing religious appeals ; and he’s a student of the civil rights movement, the legacy of which could be seen in surging Black turnout across the South after the Supreme Court rolled back parts of the Voting Rights Act.
Warnock has kept the door open on a presidential bid ; his colleague Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) is also frequently discussed as a potential candidate .

Herndon and Warnock discussed how Democrats can win in the South following election victories by Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom and others; why Warnock made the trip to Michigan to campaign for Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed; and the need for presidential leadership to resolve some of America’s toughest problems at home and abroad.

Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel .
I feel like some of the reason the South hasn’t seen some of that investment is a presumption that white Southerners are unpersuadable.

And in your race, and I think what happened in Georgia, it wasn’t just turnout, but it was also persuasion. It was convincing people to move on from Republicans and embrace Democrats. How do you make that persuasion happen?

As a pastor, there’s something that I call the ministry of presence. Sometimes you can’t solve people’s problems because they’re complicated or complex. They may take time, or you may not be able to fix it immediately. But there’s something healing about having people show up for you.

And so when I was running in 2021, and then again had to turn around and run in 2022, I would show up in these little towns all across Georgia. The folks were surprised that I was there. And you might be thinking, “Well, of course they were surprised that a Democrat was there.” No, they were surprised that anybody running for the United States Senate was in their little town.

And as we sat down and talked about their hospital that had just closed, as we talked about the struggles that their farmers were having under the tariffs that Trump imposed in his first term, we realized that we had things in common, and we shared a faith. And I got enough of those voters to build the kind of moral, multiracial coalition to win.
Some of the playbook here, though, feels kind of intuitive. You know, show up, lean in to a kind of shared identity. Campaign everywhere.

Even when I’ve heard Southerners talk about building structures over a long period of time, part of me wonders: Why has it been such an effort to make that happen? Are we talking around racism here? Is it just because these are people who have been written off?

That’s a good point, and it’s an interesting thing. Here’s what Black Southerners and white Southerners have in common — particularly poor white Southerners in these rural districts: They’re written off. Like, that’s a shared identity. And if we’re ever to have a moment in this country that transforms it into something that Dr. King called the beloved community, we’ll somehow traverse those boundaries and recognize how much we have in common and how much our interests are connected.

I thought it was really interesting how you went to Michigan to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, who obviously was victorious in that race. You made a clear pitch to Black voters. I thought it was an interesting message. I want you to just describe it — why was that advocacy important to you?

First of all, I wanted us to win the majority. But also, as I looked at that debate as it was unfolding, I had to show up. I’m a child of the Black church. And when we say the Black church, let me hasten because people don’t know this history.

We’ve never meant anything racially exclusive about that. Black church is just a moniker for the anti-slavery church. Because almost all of American Christianity acquiesced — not just acquiesced, aided and provided a kind of moral covering, if you will, for slavery. So the Black church was literally born fighting for freedom. It was born fighting bigotry.
“We need somebody who doesn’t need the job; who really is driven by a deep sense of moral vocation and mission, and for whom the job is a set of tools.”

And when I saw the all-out assault on Brother Abdul on the basis of his religious identity — bigotry is bigotry, and religious bigotry is bigotry. The Black church was born fighting bigotry. And so you literally have people saying that he’s unfit because of where he prays and how he prays.
And if there was anybody that I felt should be the tip of the spear rejecting that idea, it was the Black church, and so I went, among other things, to remind my colleagues there of who we are.

It wasn’t just Republicans who used some of those Islamophobic attacks. There was the infamous scene of Haley Stevens , the Democratic congresswoman who lost that primary, going to the Black church [with Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers].
Here she is standing with somebody who is engaged in this kind of Islamophobic rhetoric, and she’s in a Black church doing this. It’s deeply insulting.

We had Abdul El-Sayed on our show , and he made the case for cutting off aid to Israel. In 2025, you and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff voted to block a measure from Bernie Sanders that would’ve stopped $8 billion in aid for Israel.
I recently saw a stat that 74 percent of Democrats oppose additional funding for Israel, per a poll from the New York Times and Siena . Was that vote a mistake?
We’ve had several [Joint Resolution of Disapproval] votes. You chose only to mention the one that I didn’t vote for. I have voted on multiple occasions to limit military aid to Israel.

My North Star where that issue is concerned is a region where Israeli mothers and Palestinian mothers can put their children to sleep at night, know that they’re safe, and have them awaken to a world that embraces their full humanity.

I support a two-state solution. Clearly, Netanyahu does not. He is a problem. and what we need in this moment is leadership. I don’t shirk that one bit. But I will tell you this, as someone who has voted for these [joint resolutions] on a few occasions in response to the moral atrocities that we’ve seen in Gaza, I can tell you that what I’ve learned is that there is no replacement for presidential leadership, and we haven’t had that on this issue in quite some time.
Would you include President Biden in that?
We have not had the kind of leadership that I would want to see on that issue in quite some time. The people are crying out for more.
I am just old enough to remember when an American president took two old men in a room at Camp David and he wouldn’t let them go until they worked something out.

Of course, Anwar Sadat paid a very high price for that. I remember that, too. I think I was in seventh grade. We need American presidential leadership in this moment for that and for a whole range of reasons.
You’ve mentioned presidential leadership. What’s one nonnegotiable for the next Democratic presidential nominee? What’s one thing you think they have to do?

We need somebody who doesn’t need the job; who really is driven by a deep sense of moral vocation and mission, and for whom the job is a set of tools. But the mission is what is central. I think when you have somebody who’s grounded in that kind of deep commitment, then we’re onto something.

I’ve seen you kind of dodge this question about whether you’re considering a run for president in 2028. Your go-to answer was, “Well, I’m focused on the midterms.” Now that we have results from the midterms, I’m going ask you again.
Are you thinking about running for president in 2028?
I remain very committed, and deeply honored to be in this fight for the people of Georgia.
You know, who gets to represent 11 million people? Stand up, get up, fight for them every day? And I remain prayerful about what’s the best use of my gifts in this moment.
I hope that at the end of my life, I will have poured it all out and gone ’till the wheels fall off. And that’s what I’m trying to do — give it all I have.
Give me a sense of how that decision calculus works. Very few people are ever in the position to think about such a thing. How do you go about making a decision about whether that’s true for you?
I have been praying this prayer since I was a kid. I ask God to order my steps. And so you just do the work, and I think you’ll know what you need to do when the time comes.

articles.headline: New Hyundai Elantra Hybrid Debuts With 53 Mpg, AI in the Dash
keyFacts: Hyundai revealed the 2027 Elantra sedan and 2028 Elantra Hybrid at the LA Auto Show with a targeted 53 mpg for the hybrid.
The new models feature the Gleo AI voice assistant, an Android Automotive OS-based dashboard, and a larger exterior design.
Hyundai announced that the 2027 Elantra sedan is expected to arrive in early 2027, followed by the hybrid in late 2027.
body: Hyundai pulled back the cover on the new 2027 Elantra sedan and 2028 Elantra Hybrid this week at the LA Auto Show, and, wow, it looks like nothing else in its class. The bold styling may not be for everyone — though, personally, I dig it — but economy car shoppers will certainly be interested in the compact hybrid sedan’s targeted 53 mpg and Gleo, Hyundai’s new AI voice assistant that controls the automaker’s new Android Automotive OS-based dashboard tech.

The humble Hyundai Elantra hasn’t historically been a sexy car, but it remains an important one for the brand. It’s the automaker’s second-bestselling vehicle, behind only the Tucson. More importantly, the Elantra is one of the stalwarts of the affordable compact sedan class, a segment that many US automakers have abandoned in favor of more profitable SUVs. At a time when buyers are more sensitive than ever to inflated fuel costs and sticker prices, economy car options like the Elantra and its second-generation hybrid powertrain are worth our attention.
More powerful and efficient hybrid

The updated hybrid powertrain pairs a 1.6-liter four-cylinder gasoline engine with a 6-speed dual-clutch automatic gearbox. Combined output at the front wheels rises to 155 horsepower (up from 139 hp in the current car), thanks to a more powerful 45-kilowatt electric-assist motor (up from 32kW).
More from CNET

An updated regenerative braking system recaptures energy when slowing and now offers an “EV-like one-pedal driving experience” that can bring the car to a complete stop at its maximum setting. Additionally, the hybrid now features a new Stay mode that lets the climate control and infotainment systems run while parked for up to 30 minutes without firing up the gas engine.

Sharing the stage in LA, the new nonhybrid Elantra arrives with the same 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine and continuously variable transmission as the current generation. At 147 hp with a target of 35 mpg combined, it’s no more powerful than before, but it should also be no less efficient, despite the sedan’s increased size. I’d say the hybrid is the better choice, though it will likely also be the more expensive powertrain option.
Pleos Connect, Gleo AI

Inside, a new cockpit design moves the now-hoodless digital instrument cluster, a 9.9-inch “Slim Information Display,” away from the driver and toward the windshield on the dashboard. The new placement, similar to what I’ve seen on recent Toyota models, puts vehicle information closer to the driver’s line of sight.

Pleos Connect, Hyundai’s new Android Automotive OS-based infotainment suite, lives on a 12.9-inch center display. Despite being based on Android, it still features the automaker’s bespoke navigation and media software, rather than Google Maps. The system is said to be over-the-air updatable and features standard wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto for drivers who’d rather bring their own apps on the road.

The Pleos dashboard OS is matched with Gleo AI (who names these things?!), which is Hyundai’s new AI voice assistant that lets drivers and passengers talk to the car rather than occupy a hand on the touchscreen. Hyundai says the system features “contextual language support, multi-command capability and zone-specific recognition,” which basically means the car knows who’s talking to it and which seat they’re in and can assign context to voice prompts based on the situation.
Anything but anonymous

“Affordable doesn’t have to be anonymous,” said Olabisi Boyle, Hyundai’s senior vice president of product, at the unveiling. I agree: Hyundai’s designers clearly aren’t afraid to push the design envelope, and the new Elantra is anything but bland.

The sedan introduces the automaker’s Art of Steel design language, with chunky flared fenders that feel inspired by the brand’s recent new SUVs. The tall greenhouse looks a bit cartoonish if you catch it at the wrong angle, but it provides increased headroom inside. From certain angles, the sedan’s beefy fenders remind me of an angular Korean take on the Subaru WRX. From other viewpoints, I can see inspiration from Hyundai’s N Vision 74 concept and the hydrogen-fueled Nexo, particularly in the triangular rear windows.

The sedan measures 188.8 inches bumper-to-bumper on a 108.3-inch wheelbase that is 1.2 inches longer than the current model’s. Hyundai says the stretch for this generation improves rear-passenger space, now rated at 39.1 inches of legroom on the second row. The Elantra, according to its designers, now approaches the interior volume of a midsize car, a claim I’d take with a grain of salt had I not watched multiple six-foot-plus attendees slip into the back seat with relative ease.
Arriving next year

Hyundai did not announce pricing or detailed specs at the auto show debut, and availability is still vague. However, based on the stated model years, which are usually slightly offset from calendar years, I expect the 2027 Elantra sedan to arrive in early 2027, with the 2028 Elantra Hybrid following in late 2027.
Editors’ note: Antuan Goodwin’s travel costs were covered by Genesis. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

articles.headline: Can AI really help spot Black Friday deals? We put it to the test
keyFacts: BBC tests of four major AI chatbots for Black Friday deals found mixed results, including broken retailer links and inaccurate prices.
Consumer group Which? warned that inaccurate chatbot pricing wastes time for Black Friday shoppers trying to find budget deals.
Business advisor Naureen Mohammed said she suspects advertising models will start influencing future chatbot shopping recommendations.
body: - Published
Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of online woes.
Retailers promise bargains - but the sheer number of offers can leave us feeling no closer to finding the best deal.
It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.
But are they any good at finding Black Friday deals? We had a go ourselves a week ahead of the big day.
Figures suggest relatively few UK shoppers currently go to AI tools for help.
A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries found the UK ranked second-last in the proportion of people who said they had used AI to help them shop.
Crucially, 36% of respondents who said they would be shopping around Black Friday didn't plan to use an AI tool at all.
But the survey suggested a growing number of people were considering it - and tech firms have released features to capitalise on this.
Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.
In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.
But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.
We asked four models to find a 55-inch TV deal, using the free versions of many of the most popular tools.
While this was not a rigorous scientific test, the experience we had produced mixed results.
ChatGPT - full price and not available to buy
OpenAI's ChatGPT came up with four options.
Its top pick was a Hisense TV on Chinese retailer Joybuy's website, on sale for Â£499 down from Â£649.
The next recommendation was a 55-inch TCL-branded TV, but a sidebar showed prices for the 50-inch version, from Â£379 to Â£814.
Option three was the same Hisense TV as before, but for full price at Â£649 from John Lewis and Richer Sounds.
This was the "best safer purchase" according to ChatGPT, as the sites offered longer guarantee periods.
But clicking on the links did not go well. Both retailers said the TV was no longer listed online.
The fourth option was equally fruitless - another TCL TV, at full price, Â£150 over our budget and not available online.
At the bottom, ChatGPT served one last offer - "one OLED option to compare" - for a Â£1,100 LG TV that was marked as "Ad".
Claude - honest, but not too helpful
Claude produced the shortest answer of all the models we tested, and unlike the others, it did not give much detail on the specifications of each model.
Instead, it seemed to base its results on a small number of reviews published online.
It recommended the same two TCL TVs as ChatGPT.
But when we clicked on the links, they sent us to two dead pages on the Richer Sounds website.
Some other links led to year-old round-ups of Black Friday 2025 deals.
Claude was not very enthusiastic about its other two recommendations due to a lack of independent reviews - calling one "a decent option" but saying it "wouldn't pick" the other.
It also listed two Samsung TVs, but it told us not to buy them, with one "over budget and not clearly better than the TCLs".
We were left wondering why it even mentioned them in the first place.
Gemini - a familiar pattern
Different AI model, same TV manufacturers - albeit different Hisense and TCL models to the previous chatbots' recommendations.
Gemini generated a table comparing four different models, but offered no links to the stores it named, so we searched for them ourselves.
The prices for one TCL TV were correct at Â£649, but it was sold out at one of the named retailers.
It said the other TCL model was available from Argos and Currys for Â£539 - correct for Argos, but when we checked Currys, it was Â£60 more expensive.
Again, it included two Samsung models to avoid due to lower screen specs.
Alexa - accurate but limited
Alexa came back with four TVs, from its own Amazon Ember at Â£532 to a Â£699 Samsung.
But its top recommendation was to go for another Samsung model at Â£616 (down from Â£749), based on its picture quality and Amazon customer rating.
Its fourth option was for a Sony TV, but it was only 50 inches, leaving us unsure why it had included it.

All the prices stated were correct, but Amazon only searches its own store. Alexa did acknowledge this, encouraging us to check its rivals for better deals, "as prices can vary" and we could get longer guarantees elsewhere.
Inconsistent pricing
There are methods that can boost the likelihood of getting a better response, from crafting more informative prompts to upping a chatbot's "thinking" level.
Tech journalist Alex Hughes had better luck than we did when he used ChatGPT's agentic AI mode to find a TV in last year's Black Friday sales.
Agentic AI is still in its early days, but it allows AI to act with more autonomy and carry out multi-step tasks.
The search took about 20 minutes "with very little work on my end needed," Hughes wrote for Tom's Guide, external in November 2025.
A year on, he told the BBC he didn't go through with buying a TV at that time.
He did later purchase one of the seven models ChatGPT had surfaced - but he had found it for a lower price in a bricks-and-mortar shop.
Will he be using AI to find Black Friday deals again this year? "Probably not," he said.
He reckoned it saved him time, but "when you're trying to deal with something like live price data... it will be inconsistent and quite often incorrect".
Slim pickings
While we were served up the same brands again and again, in reality there are tonnes of products listed for sale around Black Friday.
Naureen Mohammed, who advises businesses on how to get their products to appear in AI results, told the BBC customers did not see the full picture when they talked to chatbots.
If businesses fail to update their prices when people start hunting for bargains, "last year's prices are served up as today's deals".
"I suspect the whole model for advertising is going to start influencing AI recommendations," she said.
Her own analysis of chatbots' Black Friday tech deals in the UK suggested the big retailers came out on top - with Amazon mentioned in half of responses, and Currys following closely behind.
Her tips include asking an assistant "is that this year's price?" and clicking on the links provided - "because you shouldn't take any advice from the AI system at face value".
But consumer group Which? recently said inaccurate pricing in AI results added more work, external to Black Friday deal-hunting.

"If you ask ChatGPT for a list of 10 laptops under Â£400 and seven of the results are priced higher, you've likely wasted a good chunk of time going through them to discover the bot gave you only three options," said senior researcher Hannah Walsh.
"The opposite is also true - you could miss out on great models in your budget if ChatGPT tells you they are more expensive than they actually are."
